Unfortunately two players (originally ranked #2 and #4) recieved a Game
Loss penalty for incorrect decklists, and couldn't participate in the
finals. This changed the scene a bit, allowing the original #6 and #7
players to play. The finals came to a quick conclusion thanks to the
number of active decks present. Seating:

Tibor Holhos (DOM OBF stealth-bleed) -> Milan Horvath (a toolboxish take
on the weenie Saturday Night Special + Dragon Breath Roungs combo) ->
Daniel Hadik-Barkoczy (playing Giovanni Powerbleed) -> Tamas Kovacs
(Malkavian stealth-bleed) -> Peter Korsos (Tzimisce Wall).

Tibor started the game straightforward bleeding Milan, who had two
Intercept locations and so actually tried to block. I influenced out
Andrea Giovanni, who started with an unfortunate bleed for 6 (which never
connected thanks to Istvan's Archon Investigation), leaving me minionless
for a few turns. Istvan seemingly had no difficulty to bypass Peter's
Intercept, and he even removed the early Smiling Jack.

Milan shot and Graverobbed Tibor's Count Ormonde, and spent most of his
effort trying to fend off his predator. A bleed for 5 at 3 stealth was
bounced all the way to Peter, who had to make the choice whom to send it
to; he chose to send it back to his predator, thanks to which during my
next turn I succesfully ousted Istvan. During his turn Tibor just managed
to finished off Milan, apparently drawing just enough bleed to do it.

I tried to play my game, and made it a point not to allow any permanent
Intercept for my prey (using blocks and DI as needed to deprive him of
this bothersome resource), and at the same time used Le Dinh Tho's special
every turn on him. Although I never got through his transient Intercept,
my efforts were enough to completely deny my prey his Intercept. Tibor
managed to oust me (again, just barely; his hand clogged on stealth due to
my no-blocks policy), and proceeded to quickly eliminate Peter, whose hand
was full of wake cards, but at that point had no intercept comparable to
the vast amount of stealth Tibor could dish out.

The game was fun and brief, but all the better; Tibor gained a well-earned
tournament win. Here's the winning deck:

Ya know, as I've been giving the circumstances of this topic a recent
think, I suspect that the problem lies in needing some further detail in
the VEKN tourney rules as to how you go about using decklists... Here is
all that we have to go on;

VEKN Rules:

6.3. Constructed Deck Registration

The head judge or tournament organizer may require players to register
their decks upon arrival at a tournament. Registration records the original
composition of each deck. Once a tournament official receives a player's
decklist, the deck may not be altered. Failure to properly register a deck
will result in the head judge applying the appropriate provisions of the
V:EKN Penalty Guidelines. The V:EKN recommends that organizers check a
reasonable number of decks against their decklists each round.

That last line is the only guide as to when and how to implement decklist
checking, and its vague. It seems like a general habit has been developed,
if decklists are used at all, the decklists of finalists are checked.
This results in the inherently unfair situation, that clerical errors are
penalized only _after_ the preliminary rounds are completed.
Consider the current tournament. had Gyula Erdos' decklist error been
discovered at any point _other_ than by a check of the decklists of the
finalists, his game loss penalty would _not_ have prevented him from
participating in the finals, _at all_. A game loss and a correction of
decklist (or deck) would still have left him with 2 GW, and some
significant number of VPs. The same may have held true for Jozsef Gal,
too, depending upon the round of discovery for the discrepancy.

And this seems to come from the arbitrary determination someone made
somewhere along the line that 'Reasonable'=5 when the finals and decklists
are concerned. By this point in the tournament, a Game Loss penalty is IMO
a much higher penalty than the Judge's Guide intends (since the Judge's
Guide considers a generic "round" independent of which , as it is only
being consistently applied for the Final Round.

As a hypothetical, if a Judge could apply two different penalties;
1. Preliminary Round Game Loss, or
2. Final Round Game Loss

Written out that way, it becomes clear that the latter is an incredibly
stiff penalty (nearly as bad as a disqualification, IMO), whereas the first
is certainly bad, but not insurmountable. The policy of checking
finalists' decklists, only, creates just such an artificially high penalty,
and only by virtue of the timing of implementation.
For certain, Finalist decklist checks are, strictly speaking, a legal
interpretation of the Rules, but that seems to me to be only because the
rules are so vague on the subject. I think it would be really beneficial
if some further detail were written into the VEKN Rules to prevent this
from occuring (either by differentiating between GLs in prelims vs. finals
in terms of penalty level, or by providing additional guidelines on
implementing decklist checks). Choosing to implement this part of the VEKN
Rules in this manner, though, is not in keeping with the spirit of honest
competition, since they more often than not exclude the _proven_ best VTES
players of the tournament, on the basis of clerical skills, and not game
play.

Done, now... sorry if I crushed somebody's soapbox ;-)

Regards
DaveZ

Yeah, I'd think that if these rules (i.e. deck list checks) were going
to be used and then result in folks being excluded from the finals as a
result, that either:

A) The actual deck list/check rules should be written more
comprehensively.

or

B) The deck checking should happen across the board and not right before
the finals. Check everyone's deck before the first round, see if they
match, and if they don't, make them fix them. And then check the
finalists again before they hit the final round if you really want.

The second option is much more of a pain in the ass, but if you are
going to insist on deck lists and deck checks, you should do this in
such a way as to not penalize folks too much for typos, and checking a
deck right before the final round, discovering a typo, and then kicking
someone out of the finals as a result seems like a really less optimal
way to handle this sort of thing.

On Apr 10, 3:59 am, "Joscha" <joscha.du...@gmx.de> wrote:
> Hmm, that's really a good point. On the other hand is it really that
> difficult to write a correct list? You just have to order similar
> cards together and write their number on a paper.

Sure. It isn't that difficult to write a correct list. But you also
can lose cards, accidentally leave cards in your box, leave a Haven
Uncovered on someone, write "scouting mission" as opposed to "spying
mission", or whatever. Or just change your deck at the last second and
forget to adjust the list.

> Checking ALL decklists before first round is not manageable. Maybe the
> best solution is to play without decklists at all.

It probably is. I have never in my life been to a tournament that
required deck lists. Ever. In playing competetive VTES for, like, 12
years. Anywhere. And never have I felt as if my opponents were going
to cheat as a result.

> But then you have to accept cheating through the tournament and
> deckchanging to respond to the metagame. I don't know what's better.

I don't know that I actually have to accept that. Do you honestly
think that *that* many people are changing their decks in mid
tournament? Really?

Given the situation at hand--the guys that got DQed from the final had
already turned in deck lists. Do you think they specifically and
intentionally changed their decks *after* turning in deck lists?
Knowing that if they got into the finals, their decks would be checked
against their lists? Does it really seem likely that they
intentionally changed their decks in mid tournament? I mean, yeah, ok,
it is certainly *possible*. But it strikes me as wildly unlikely. So
the end result is that these guys get DQed from the finals due to a
clerical error. Which seems kind of extreme.

I know this has come up before (again and again), but do folks really
think that there are so many people out there who are going to change
their decks mid tournament that deck lists are helpful? And even if
they think they are helpful:

A) People can be DQed for clerical errors.

B) If folks know that they only are going to get checked if they get
into the finals, what is to stop them from changing their decks until
they get in the finals, and then changing it back?

C) Folks can cheat in many, many other ways that have nothing at all
to do with deck changing. If you are so worried about cheating, how do
you stop folks from other forms of cheating? Why laser focus on this
one, yet not, like, force everyone to count their opponent's pool at
the start of each game or make sure a judge observes whenever someone
moves their pool when they are bled?

-Peter

Again again again. Please don't conflate these two issues. They are
totally separate. The continued mixing of the two is part of why we have
excessive penalties being applied for typos. A decklist error on its own
is not evidence of cheating. Cheating is horrible. Cheating is bad. If
you catch a cheater, punish them as Cheaters. DISQUALIFY CHEATERS, and
report them as such. The fact that you catch them through their decklist
does NOT mean you are supposed to apply a deck error-game loss. If we
separate the catching of cheaters from the checking of decklists, then it
becomes more clear that decklist checks (again, without associated
evidece of cheating) are being over-penalized.

Decklist error alone != cheating, as you've made clear by your two
examples above.

Decklist error, plus other evidence may = cheating.

Jozsef was missing a Coven from his deck that was on the decklist, and
had two Life in the Cities that weren't. As I understood it, the former
wouldn't have been reason to GL him (cards that change control are bound
to get lost every now and then), and later the card was found mingled in
someone elses deck. He was DQ-ed based on the missing registration of
the Lifes.

Gyula was missing a Reunion Kamut from his deck (compared to the decklist),
and was GL-ed based on this.

Concerning the points made... I think it's easy to see the reasoning why a
final GL is too harsh for a clerical error. Although I'm probably among
the more organized players, and haven't yet made any errors in decklists,
I fully understand that typos and errors in counting can happen to
everyone, and I sure as hell wouldn't want to lose the chance to play in
the finals because of a typo. Therefor I'm not very married to the idea
of decklists myself.

However, there are a number of counterarguments to be made, even in
tournaments where the decklists are only checked before the finals.

My main concern is that if you accept a certain type of deviation
(remember,
issuing anything below GL has no effect once in the finals), then you are
basically tolerating/encouraging people to commit those deviations. Saying
that "up to 3 cards difference is only a Warning" is more or less equal to
saying "you can change 3 cards for the final". Same goes with all types of
transgressions. Especially since in a tournament of sufficient size there
is little reason to change anything on one's deck before reaching the
finals, as until then there is probably zero knowledge of the opponents
decks.

I'm still not too happy about GLing players for clerical mistakes, however,
I'm not sure how to reasonably go about having decklists if there is no
consequences for a discrepancy. One possibility is to look at the decklist
and have the player restore it fully, with no penalty issued (though this
may encourage illegible decklists). Another is to simply drop having
decklists at all, and assume that the harm done by disqualifying a player
who makes an honest mistake is more than the benefit from the deterrent
factor of players knowing that their decklists will be checked.

--
Regards,

Daneel

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
Looks like my past Magic judging experience is going to help me here,
since the relevant VEKN Tournament Rules and Penalty Guidelines (and
their philosophy) are almost completely the same as they were in Magic
several years ago. Looks like they didn't change at all since the
times when V:TES was a game of Wizards.
Actually, the penalties' meaning is quite different, though. In Magic,
typical tournament is 4-6 Swiss rounds, and each round can have up to
3 games, so the term "Game Loss" is much less a penalty than in VTES.
The VTES "Game Loss" is closer to the Magic "Match Loss", but as long
as we're playing only 3 rounds, it's even more harsh.

Nevertheless, I completely agree with the judge's decision in this
case. Missing ANY cards from the deck is NOT a clerical error. When a
player writes "Scouting Mission" instead of "Spying Mission", and
there is no Dominate in his deck, this is a clerical error. If a
player wrote 11 Giant's Blood (instead of 1), it's a clerical error.
If some cards are missing, it isn't.
The decklist is the most important document of a player. Its existence
should force players to forget about the "last changes" made upon the
deck scouting, the "sideboarding" and similar things. A good judge
should make deckchecks at least sometimes, and the tournament rules
recommend the judge to check the legality of all decklists during the
first round - at least, you can check number of cards (60-90), number
of vampires (12+) and existence of banned cards. You can also notice
the most obvious clerical errors (like the mentioned 11 Giant's
Bloods). You can also ask your players to count and write the number
of cards in their libraries, and then check whether your number
correspond to theirs or not.
The decklist MUST be filled correctly and it MUST correspond to the
deck all the time. It's like a passport or driving license. A document
issued to Adam Baker will not work if you are Adam Maker - so why a
decklist with 6 Governs should work for a person with 5 Governs? You
may wonder why the penalty for Illegal Deck and Illegal Decklist is so
harsh, but I don't. Decklist mechanism is "the primary defense line"
against possible cheating, and everyone is responsible for providing a
legal decklist and starting each game with the deck corresponding to
the decklist. Yes, some cards like Haven Uncovered are usually played
on the other player's minions, so they can be lost - but, again, each
player is responsible for collecting them after each game. No excuses
here! After all, in Magic cards are often moved between the main deck
and the sideboard, but the penalty for "Procedural Error: Failure to
De-Sideboard" is still the same - Game Loss.
Considering that Game Loss in VTES means much more than in Magic, I
wouldn't probably issue it in a small tournament, but ECQ with 53
players is not a small tournament! In Magic terms, it should be REL 3
or 4 (REL stands for Rules Enforcement Level). Current Magic Penalty
Guidelines recommend to issua a GL for Illegal Decklist and Illegal
Deck at all RELs, but a few years ago they recommended Match Loss at
higher RELs, which is close enough to the GL in VTES. I've issued such
Match Loss at the Russian Nationals to a player with 59 cards in his
decklist. Yes, I know that Magic is a different game, but who said
that VTES players should not be as organized as Magic players are?
All that said, a judge should do his best to discover deck problems
BEFORE finals. Check all decklists during the first round - I've
found countless errors during such checks. Make the deckchecks. A good
way is asking all players to count their cards at the beginning of
round 2 and compare the values with your results during the decklist
checking. You should examine the decks with differences immediately,
and so on. But if the problem was encountered only prior to the final
round, a judge really should issue Game Loss.

criminal countries.

>

> think that there are so many people out there who are going to change
> their decks mid tournament that deck lists are helpful? And even if
> they think they are helpful:
>
> A) People can be DQed for clerical errors.

Missing cards are NOT clerical errors. It's too easy to cheat with
"forgetting" Fear of Mekhet, for instance, if you don't expect IC/
Justicars in the next round. So, the recommended penalty is GL, which
is right.
Once I've issued a GL to my friend's wife - she wrote "22 Lands"
instead of "22 Mountains" in her decklist. Though both my friend and
his wife later pretended that it was a clerical error, actually it
wasn't: with "22 Lands" in your decklist you can put ANY lands in your
deck, which is a way to the potential cheating. Writing "Scouting
Mission" instead of "Spying Mission" IS a clerical error, if it's
obvious that Scouting Mission cannot be in that deck.

> B) If folks know that they only are going to get checked if they get
> into the finals, what is to stop them from changing their decks until
> they get in the finals, and then changing it back?

Surely, a good judge should try to discover the possible problems
ASAP. And he should inform the players that he can make a deckcheck in
EACH round.

> C) Folks can cheat in many, many other ways that have nothing at all
> to do with deck changing. If you are so worried about cheating, how do
> you stop folks from other forms of cheating? Why laser focus on this
> one, yet not, like, force everyone to count their opponent's pool at
> the start of each game or make sure a judge observes whenever someone
> moves their pool when they are bled?
>

Because it's much more difficult to cheat these ways. Players are
going to notice such behaviour and report to the judge. First time the
judge may believe that it was unintentional, second time he will DQ
the cheater.

Yours,
Ector

for a GL.

Because it's a part of a judge's job. He must consider the POSSIBILITY
of cheating of any player. He doesn't have to talk about this, sure,
but he must think about this. And in any case like this, he should
think according to the following pattern:

1). Do I believe that player cheated? If yes, DQ him.
2). Do I believe that player's improper behaviour could possibly lead
to the cheating (or can be a well-masked cheating)? If yes (and in
most cases it's so), apply the recommended penalty (GL in this case).
3). If the player's behaviour could not possibly lead to the cheating,
a small penalty should be issued (warning, for instance). This is a
niche of "clerical errors" and similar things.

and there are guardians to prevent this.
As well, I cannot believe that all VTES players are angels that are
genetically incapable of cheating, and there are judges to prevent
such behaviour. Nothing to complain about, they just do their job. And
if you try to go onto the airplane with your old trusted .44 Magnum,
you are going to have serious problems - as well as if you try to play
an incomplete deck in VTES tournament. You know the rules, you know
their sense, and obeying them isn't that difficult.

> No CCG can be a serious sport without decklists, IMHO.

IMHO a card game cannot be considered a sport. VTES is a game. It is a
fun, serious competitive game at times, but still it's a game. Then
again, I've always had trouble with golf being considered a sport as
well...go ahead flame away :) I consider both to be enjoyable games of
skill, but if the activity itself isn't enough physical exertion to
make you sweat (playing cards without air-conditioning in the summer
doesn't count) then it really can't be considered a sport.

Now to get back on topic for a second; I do agree that rules exist for
a reason and dislike playing with people that intentionally disregard
the rules (especially play to win). I have no problem making a
decklist if it is required for a tournament, but I do not agree that
it is a prerequisite for a serious game of VTES. But if decklists are
going to be used to verify deck contents I think it could be done in a
better manner than only checking decks prior to the finals. If
decklist checks are going to be done, have it as part of the
registration process. Check all decks when the decklist is turned in.
Then do a few random (or targeted if you suspect deck changing) checks
(whatever time permits) at the beginning of each round. This way you
can catch the accidents and clerical errors up front instead of
kicking people out of the finals and you also show that you are
serious about people not changing decks during the tournament if that
happens to concern your playgroup.

> But we were seriously thinking about to drop the decklist checking for
> the next ECQ, or greater tournaments.
>

That's one option. Even without my crusade for change, simply a different
strategy for decklist checks could be sufficient. How's this for a
different definition of 'Reasonable' wrt decklist checks?

Decklist checks: Before each of the three preliminary rounds, 15% of the
field of players will be randomly selected for decklist checks. All errors
discovered will result in issuing a formal warning penalty, and the
correction of the deck's contents to reflect the decklist (assuming said
decklist is legal).
Before the finals, all finalist decks will be submitted to the Head
Judge. Decks will be checked against decklist contents, and if errors are
discovered, a formal warning will be issued, and the deck contents will be
corrected to reflect what is written in the decklist (assuming said
decklist is legal). [In the case of illegal decklists, the judge will use
his discretion to adjust contents to make a legal deck.*] The Head Judge
will set up the Finals table, once the players have chosen their seating
order. No player may make contact with his deck before being seated for
the start of the final round. An additional 5 minutes is allowed for
shuffling between seating and the start of the finals.

There. The above achieves Perfect prevention of cheating in the finals
through changes to deck contents. No one can cheat through card changes in
the finals (unless they try to so under the scrutiny of the Judge during
the 5 minute shuffling period), as they will know their decks will be
checked and adjusted to reflect the decklist submitted at the start of the
tourney. No clerical errors will result in someone not being able to play
either (unless they already had a multitude of warnings in the prelims),
although they will rightly be forced to play with a perhaps sub-optimal
deck.

[*] This part needs further work, I recognize... Consider the brackets a
place-holder for a better defined policy.

Messages.Author: wumpus

Howdy,

Ector wrote:

> Rules are not stupid, and if everyone
> will follow them, no problems will arise.

I just wanted to excerpt this out, as it 1) was a very frightening
attitude to me, and 2) really seems to encapsulate the clash of
culture - more effectively, I think, than the 'innocent until proven
guilty' (or not) framing.

The assertion appears to be 'No rule is (ever) stupid, and, further,
if we all follow rules unquestioningly, everyone will be better off.'
This is totalitarian thinking at its most essential; it raises the
stakes over the familiar (Western) cliche 'if you're not doing
anything wrong, you have nothing to hide', as it seeks to validate
authority to the highest degree possible. I find it fairly
astonishing that anyone, even or especially someone who has presumably
directly experienced life in a totalitarian state, would endorse this
line of argument.

On the actual subject of decklists: I guess I agree that decklists
shouldn't be such a hurdle, and are a reasonable check against
cheating. OTOH, they are clearly an inconvenience as well, and the
implementation of checking seems to leave something to be desired. It
is a tradeoff (rather analogous to the security checking now in force
at US airports - it inconveniences everyone, some very greatly, for
limited benefit). The real question is whether the inconvenience is
worth the benefit.

Alex

tournament without decklists is beyond my imagination, but if LSJ
himself runs such tournaments, the game ISN'T A SERIOUS SPORT anymore,
and it isn't going to become a serious sport in the near future.

This is the real reason of all this hassle. The game has Judge's
Guidelines written in times when it was a real sport (or at least was
supposed to be a real sport), but it isn't a real sport anymore. A
Hungarian judge issued a penalty according to the rules, so why would
anyone complain about this? A good sportsman should think: "Those
players are obviously should train better to avoid being penalized for
such violation of the rules", but there are no good sportsmen here.
Most people here think: "I could be penalized such way as well", and
this makes them write stupid things about "draconian rules", "clerical
errors" and so on - instead of learning by example.

Please look at the current VEKN Judge's Guidelines.

-----------------------------------------------------------
102. Deck Problem - Illegal Main Deck (Legal Decklist)

Definition:

This penalty applies to tournaments in which decklists are being used.
This penalty applies to players who have misplaced cards from their
deck or have cards from a previous game in their deck.

<....skipped...>

**** The contents of the main deck do not match the decklist. ****

Philosophy:

The decklist is the ultimate guide to a player's deck. If the decklist
indicates a legal deck, but the actual contents of the deck do not
match the decklist, the player should restore the deck to reflect the
decklist. If the judge can determine with complete confidence that the
deck/decklist discrepancy is due to an error on the decklist (a player
is using an all Gangrel deck and has Campground Hunting Ground listed
on the decklist instead of Zoo Hunting Ground), he or she may decide
to fix the decklist instead. A warning should be issued in this case.

Penalty:

Game loss, and then be instructed to make any changes necessary to
make the contents of the deck match what is recorded on the decklist.
The changes must be complete before the next round begins for the
player to continue in the tournament.
------------------------------------------------------------

Now tell me ANYBODY, what's wrong with this rule? It's absolutely
clear and simple, its philosophy is explained well enough, and don't
tell me about "draconian rules", "Magic experience" and similar shit.
It's a rule of YOUR game. Why don't you wish to obey it? Why can
anybody even think that he shouldn't get a GL if he would forget a
Haven Uncovered in other player's deck in the previous round? Careful
tracking of your deck is your RESPONSIBILITY as a player at serious
event. Failure to restore the deck to its original status (as stated
in the decklist) is a dangerous behaviour that's potentially
disruptive to the event, without even talking about the possible
cheating, and it MUST be penalized.
I can agree that GL may be too harsh penalty, but not at the highest-
level events like ECQ or Nationals where all participants are supposed
to be the best sportsmen available. And note that even without GL the
guilty player would be forced to restore the deck to reflect the
decklist. The rule also describes what is the "clerical error", and
what isn't. "Campground Hunting Ground" instead of "Zoo Hunting
Ground" is a clerical error, 6 Reunion Kamuts instead of 5 isn't.
According to the rule, extra RK should be removed from the deck EVEN
if the judge decides to issue a warning instead of GL.
I must also note that GL in the finals is still very, very different
from the DQ, since DQ should lead to the further investigation by VEKN
officials and the investigation usually leads to BANNING the guilty
player for some period of time.

Now, I'm completely pissed off to see how the disorganized players
(even the most experienced) are trying to change the rule instead of
trying to change their playstyle. If the road police officer would
issue you a fine for driving too fast, would you try to change the
laws? Would you demand to remove the road policemen from the streets?
Or to take their radars away, so they couldn't measure your driving
speed? I guess not, since this would be extremely stupid. But players
actually DO assault the good judge for issuing the RIGHT penalty, they
are actually trying to change the rules, and they SERIOUSLY advice to
remove decklists to make the bad and disorganized play
undetectable!!!

And the worst part of it is LSJ's behaviour. He is responsible to
protect the good judge against these stupid "suggestions" and dirty
talks. "The law is harsh, but it's the law". When the good judges
become subjects of such pressure, it's impossible to enforce the rules
anymore. But as long as LSJ himself runs tournaments without
decklists, I guess that the law isn't working anymore, and nobody
considers VTES a serious sporting game. Everything is already lost,
and nothing to do here for me.

Yours,
Ector

Messages.Author: Teeka
Messages.Body:
As you all know by now, I'm not a tourney player. But nevertheless, I
strongly believe in the need for clear rules and strict enforcing of
those rules when playing competively, in order to ensure optimal game-
quality. Not just in games like this, but sports as well. So here's my
2 cents:

For what it's worth, I agree with Janne on the point that decklists
don't stop cheating, only one form of cheating.
I do think, however, that any measures possible to stop a possible way
of cheating should be enforced. To go with his copy protection thing:
just because there's other ways to break the law, doesn't mean we
should just abandon all laws. That would be the worst possible thing
to do.
Same with VTES: we must try and do anything we can, and issue as many
laws as we can, to stop cheating as much as possible. Same with real
life: laws expand and update constantly, along with the breakers' ways
of breaking them. And yes, the cheaters will always be one step ahead.
That doesn't mean the law-abiding should stop caring about, or
reacting to that.

I agree strongly with Ector on this: players should look after their
decks. I mean, come on, how hard is it to count (and re-count) the
amount of cards in your deck after a game?! How hard is it to double-
check the card-names and amounts you've written down on a form? We're
talking about being able to correctly write down, and check, what 102
game cards you have with you. It will take you 3 minutes max to make
absolutely sure everything is in order, so what's the problem?

The "Haven Uncovered-thing" can easily be resolved by keeping your
cards in sleeves that have coloured backs. You can spot a cards that's
not yours (and find the deck it's supposed to be in) instantly just by
turning your decks over. If it so happens two players use the same
colour sleeves, that's just more incentive to count and re-count after
a game. Again, how hard is it to do this?

I think that failing to do a few simple things like filling in a form
correctly and making sure your deck is in order means you're either
cheating, or incredibly lazy/sloppy. In both cases I think you
shouldn't complain if you get DQ'd.
F1 drivers get DQ'd if their car is not in order. Soccer players
cannot enter the field if their outfit is not in order, or if they're
not on the team list. Boxers cannot enter a match if they're too
heavy. So they make sure everything is ok beforehand, as they know no
possible excuse will make things different. It's perfectly normal for
any competition to have such rules.

Teeka

Learning what by example? That it is somehow useful to saddle your

'Cause it is absurd to get a GL for forgetting a Haven Uncovered. It

This has nothing at all to do with disorganization. It has to do with
rationality. Decklists don't actually accomplish much other than
provide another hurdle to folks who are already on the fence about
going to a tournament. And occasionally result in folks getting
effectively DQed for misplacing cards by accident.

> and they SERIOUSLY advice to
> remove decklists to make the bad and disorganized play
> undetectable!!!

Bad and disorganized play does not become undetectable due to a lack
of decklists. What becomes undetectable is the occasional
mislplacement of cards and the occasional dubious attempt to gain
advantage by swapping cards around which very few people are going to
do in the first place, and for the people who do do this, it is rarely
actually going to help them. You have played in a VTES tournament
before, right?

> And the worst part of it is LSJ's behaviour.

What--he pointed out that the decklist rules are optional, 'cause they
are?

> He is responsible to
> protect the good judge against these stupid "suggestions" and dirty

"Dirty talks"? What are you even talking about here? The general
consensus here is that decklists are mostly unecessary. 'Cause they
are. What are "dirty talks"?

> But as long as LSJ himself runs tournaments without
> decklists, I guess that the law isn't working anymore,

The "law" works just fine. The VEKN tournament rules don't require
decklists. And most folks running tournaments (well, at least in the
US--I can't really speak for the rest of the world) tend to lean
towards the optional nature of this rule and ignores it. 'Cause they
realize that it doesn't accomplish much, is a hassle, and can cause as
much damage as it prevents.

-Peter

On 12 apr, 16:31, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> I'd be curious how much difference one card makes in the liklihood of
> drawing it.

That's not the point. The point is that certain agreements (if not
rules) are made about the material used to play the game. Of course
one extra or missing card in a 90 card decks does not make a huge
difference. But if you'd allow that, then how about two cards? How
about three? If no clear line can be drawn as to the specific point
where these things start giving a player an advantage , then you have
no choice but to disallow them altogether.

> > And FYI, people have been disqualified from the Tour de France (and
> > the like) lots of times because of incorrectly filled out forms.
>
> I challenge you to find one, though, where the participant was pulled from
> the event for a form error, after being allowed to start (nevermind almost
> finish) the race.
>

There'd be none, probably, because the whole form-business gets done
REAL carefully. I know for sure that if Lance's team-boss had
forgotten to put his name on the appearence-list for the final day,
he'd be screwed. So the boss makes 100% sure that doesn't happen.
Entire (less careful) teams have been disallowed to start because of
clerical errors though. Other "minor" errors, like a bicycle that's
not been built to regulations, or missing a urine-test, have been
known to DQ a cyclist even at the final day.

Cyclists have also been known to get DQ'd even during a race, due to
other rule-breaking such as changing to a non-regulation bike during
the race or not keeping a "straight course" during a sprint to the
finish.

You shouldn't compare the decklist-thing to filling in a form at the
Tour. Instead, you should compare tinkering with your bike during a
Tour (or missing a urine-test or something) to changing your deck
during an event. It's not enough that things are ok at the start,
things get checked during the course of a Tour on a daily basis. And
it also doesn't matter if you actually gained an advantage or if you
did things deliberately. Breaking the rules = breaking the rules.

In that case, Teeka, we should ensure that all tournaments have 2
Judges for every player: One to handle their hand, and one to handle
all their cards and counters in play. That way, no players are able to
modify the contents of their deck, the quantity of their pool, the
amount of blood on their minions, etc. All cheating will be stopped.
Oh, also, all players will be required to communicate with their hand-
judge one at a time in an opaque soundproof booth to prevent them from
being scouted. Oh, also, all Judges must wear opaque masks and gloves,
vocal distorters, lumpy clothing to further help disguise their
identities, and everything a Judge says must be recorded and replayed
by the head judge to help prevent collusion.

Or did you perhaps mean we should do anything *reasonable* to stop
cheating? If you look at the amount of work all players have to do to
make decklists and the amount of work a judge must do to collect and
secure them and the amount of work the judge must do to check them
against decks and the amount of time the players have to waste waiting
for the judge to check them and the cost of the judge having to
penalize players whose decklists do not match their decks due to error
and compare that with the amount of cheaters caught by decklist
checking and the amount of cheaters dissuaded by decklist checking, I
am confident that the costs of decklists are NOT reasonable under
almost any circumstances.

I think the rules changes should be that if you require decklists, you
should be required to do exactly what you detail above:

Check decks at the beginning of tournament. All players must have a
deck that matches their decklist at that time - either by modifying
their deck, or modifying their list.

But it *does* harass oridinary consumers, who want to copy a CD they bought
for their car stereo and their computer at work. Or play a computer game on
their laptop while they travel, without having to pack all the original game
CDs and DVDs - not because they're needed to play the game, but because the

You are correct. It isn't a huge amount of work. But it is an extra
hurdle for the less committed players--VTES is a pretty fringe game. I
mean, like, yeah, we love it and all, but it is hardly like people are
knocking down walls to get into tournaments in most places. A lot of
people who come to VTES tournaments are already fairly "on the
fence"--i.e. they like the game, but aren't real committed to it, know
they are likely going to lose, and any extra impediment will likely have
them go "Uh, nah, I'm gonna go out to a movie instead" come tournament
time. Which isn't the only reason why decklists are not really
necessary, but it certainly factors in, along with (most importantly),
it doesn't really do much and is just as likely to punish someone for an
accident/clerical error as it is for intentional cheating. It is a
hassle for the players. It is a hassle for the judges (to have to
collect and check decks--this is going to add a not insignificant amount
of time to an already long event; yet another hurdle for the less
committed). It only theoretically prevents one form (and likely the
least effective) of potential cheating. It is just all around not worth
the effort it takes.

Ector did bring up a potentially solvent point about decklists--it might
make people more disciplined in regards to the game, in that they really
need to pay attention to their deck lists and count their cards after
every game and make sure everything is on the up and up at all times out
of fear of accidental DQing. That being said, I don't know that this is
necessarily something that anyone is actually going to *benefit* from in
the world of VTES, and just like every other point in regards to deck
lists, is probably not worth the hassle.

> I have no idea how much cheating gets prevented by this, just saying
> it's a way of at least trying to prevent (some) cheating.

Sure, it is. But so is having a judge count everyone's pool count at the
start of each game. And so is giving each player a screen so that no one
can peer at their hand of cards. But both of these are pretty much
extreme and absurd. Yet are still ways to prevent some cheating. Deck
lists and checks *might* prevent some cheating once and a while. And
they also might unfairly DQ someone for an honest accident once and a
while. And most of the time, they aren't going to do either (even if
this form of cheating *is* going on at the same time). But they *always*
will be kind of a hassle and an extra hurdle for folks.

Peter D Bakija

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
Looks like I've considered my goal to make VTES a true sport game
unreachable yesterday. Somebody may think that I'm afraid of the work.
It would be a shame! No, I don't afraid of the work. And, frankly, I
don't care whether LSJ or somebody else considers VTES a serious sport
game or not. For me, it's a sport game, so I'm going to develop it as
a sport game here in Minsk. Just leaving the game would be too simple.
Every player is welcome here, but please be ready to fill the
decklists and don't blame me if you get a penalty for illegal deck or
illegal decklist. We are playing seriously here - at least, we are
trying to. And we are going to have our first Nationals this year!

I never thought that I would have to explain in detail why decklists
are needed (especially to LSJ - oh my!) But as long as there are
people who don't understand this, here you are.

1). If you have decklists, you can prevent cheating with changing the
decks, at least theoretically, and everybody knows that. If you don't
have them, you cannot prevent such cheating or even discover it. And
everybody knows that you cannot! Any player willing to cheat with his
deck may do this freely.
This psychological effect is cumulative over time. If you NEVER play
with the decklists, some player may even fail to realize that changing
his deck during a tournament is cheating! Honestly, why the player
should realize this if nobody did ever check his deck? Most players
aren't "rule geeks". On the other side, if you ALWAYS play with the
decklists, if you explained the underlying philosophy and the
penalties to your players, and if you make deckchecks regularly, your
players will quickly get accustomed to check their decklist carefully
prior to submitting them, to count their cards after each round, and
so on. In other words, they will become a well-disciplined players.
2). Every player tend to consider his decklists as a "contract"
between himself and the judge. Player is responsible for playing the
submitted deck in each round of tournament, judge is responsible for
checking this and punishing the players who violate the "contract".
The mere existence of decklist and the POSSIBILITY of deckcheck makes
the players to be much more accurate, even if you don't make any
deckchecks at all! Quite often, the decklists are the most obvious
sign of a serious tournament (compared to the "friendly" tournament):
"Wow, the judge requires a decklist! Looks like it isn't going to be a
friendly casual gaming..."
3). If you have the decklists, you can help any player to restore his
deck to the original state. Players regularly forget the exact
contents of their decks, and they regularly ask me for their
decklists. With the list, a player can recall his deck in a few
second. If the judge won't have decklists, he would look incredibly
silly, since he would be unable to help the player. Decklists are
useful to the players, too - not only to the judge!
I guess that nobody cares about restoring the decks to their original
state at the tournaments without decklists, and players can play
everything they want :) Note that the players playing with incorrect
or incomplete decks are actually cheating, but they have no other
choice! This is going to further soften the border between the honest
play and cheating - if the border ever existed in the tournaments
without decklists.
4). If you have the decklists, you can quickly answer the questions
like "Does he really have Fear of Mekhet in his deck?" Five seconds,
and the answer is ready - either yes, or DQ :) If you don't have
decklists, nobody would even ask you such question - obviously you
know nothing! The judge without decklists is a pitiful judge, and his
possibilities are very limited.
5). If you have the decklists, you can easily judge the complicated
PTW questions that usually require evaluation of the player's deck.
Take the decklist and decide whether the player can "reasonably" hope
to get more than 1VP or not. Without the decklist a judge will be
forced to analyze the actual deck, which is much more difficult and
lengthy.
6). The claim that decklists prevent only one kind of cheating is
wrong. If the judge suspects that some player can be cheating, his
decklist may provide a lot of hints about the ways he may be cheating.
If you see a decklist with 10 Governs and 8 vampires with 7 capacity,
you may suspect that the player isn't playing Govern on the younger
vampire and check it. Every experienced judge will have many different
examples of possible cheating or misrepresentation that can be
suspected from the decklist.

Overall, when a judge runs a tournament without decklists, it usually
means "nothing really matters to me" attitude, and the very attitude
is very disruptive to the tournament. If you don't have decklists, do
you need a judge at all, and for what purpose? Some good players can
answer all rules questions even without a judge.
The advantages of decklists far outweights the "hassle". Seriously. As
soon as your players will get accustomed to them, you will never think
about playing a serious tournament without them.

This is very, very strange. Decklists are not just a useless papers.
They really help a lot, BOTH players and judges. They really prevent a
lot of cheating (and I don't believe that "there are no cheating in

> > No CCG can be a serious sport without decklists.
>

> > How can a serious judge even think about playing a serious

>

> occasionally get folks DQed for clerical errors. I suspect at about

I completely disagree with you about the usefulness of decklists - see

> Again with the "serious sport". No one claims that VTES is a "serious
> sport". It is a game that folks take seriously and play competetively.
Actually, I meant right that. I'm not going to become the professional

> > supposed to be a real sport), but it isn't a real sport anymore.

Issuing a GL for a deck problem at the large tournament is OK.

> > Most people here think: "I could be penalized such way as well", and
> > this makes them write stupid things about "draconian rules", "clerical
> > errors" and so on - instead of learning by example.
>
> Learning what by example? That it is somehow useful to saddle your

Learning by example for players: "I should carefully examine my deck
prior to submitting it, and be sure to have my actual deck to

Judge should learn that he needs to implement some ways to detect the

It is "optional" only if you don't have decklists at all. If you have

Hungarian judge was absolutely right when he issued GL.

>

> > anybody even think that he shouldn't get a GL if he would forget a
> > Haven Uncovered in other player's deck in the previous round?
>
> 'Cause it is absurd to get a GL for forgetting a Haven Uncovered. It
> is much less absurd to say "Huh. I forgot a Haven Uncovered. How bout

Actually, I tried to ask what makes the players to raise against the
rule. Your words about "over-penalization the clerical process"
convinced me that most players don't understand the philosophy of this
rule. Please read once more. If the judge discovers a difference
between a deck and a decklist, then he should follow the next pattern:

1). If you believe that it was cheating, DQ that player.
2). If you don't believe in cheating, but it could possibly be a
cheating, issue the recommended penalty (GL or your "VP loss"). This
is actually something AVERAGE between a warning and DQ. You cannot
issue DQ since you don't believe that it was a cheating, but you
cannot issue a warning too, since it would encourage the possible
cheating. I'd say that VP loss would suffice for minor tournaments,
but for the large tournaments like ECQ Game Loss is quite normal.
3). If the difference could not possibly be a cheating (clerical error
etc), issue warning. Let me comment this a bit. "Campground Hunting
Groung" instead of "Zoo Hunting Ground" cannot possible be a cheating,
so it's a clerical error and deserves a warning. 6 Reunion Kamuts
instead of 5 is NOT a clerical error, since a player could have 5 or
6, and changing the number during the tournament can provide some
illegal advantage to him. That's why the player really deserves a Game
Loss.

Yours,
Ector

Ector wrote:
> On Apr 13, 2:15 pm, "Bram Vink" <jja.v...@hccnet.nl> wrote:

>> bored. That doesn't change with decklists. :P
> This depends on a judge, really :) But I cannot understand why should
> a good judge run tournaments without decklists.
>

I am not convinced that decklists are necessary, but I can see a reason
for them also. I don't agree with the "hassle" argument from a player's
standpoint - I use FELDB and it's no big deal to come up with a deck list.

However, from a judge's point of view, I don't really like them.

One time I ran a tournament wherein everyone had to switch decks each
round. In that tourney, everyone was required to submit a decklist. I
did that so that everyone would be comfortable with letting others play
with their rares or what have you. Because the point of the decklists
was to prevent stealing, not cheating, I checked every deck against it's
decklist prior to the start of the tournament. And then each player was
responsible for checking their decks upon it getting returned to them.

I remember that a)checking in the decks was a pain - I was the only
judge, and there were around 15-20 players, b) people are sloppy
writers, adding to the pain, c) people are not organized in how they
write out their decks, adding to the pain, and d) it took at least half
an hour to verify all decks vs decklists, mostly due to b & c above. A
few of the players used ELDB (this was before Davila gave up on it) to
print out. But most didn't. And many of the decks weren't in the order
they were on their decklists. THAT was a real pain.

In the end, the deck lists weren't really used, because no one ended up
missing any of their cards. But that doesn't prove that they did not
have a preventative effect in keeping folks from walking off with a
disarm by mistake.

As a judge however, I wouldn't really want to do decklist checks of all
of the decks prior to a tournament, just because they are a pain. I
don't think they are a hassle for players, but for me, they were a pain.
If I had a couple of other non-playing judges, I might consider doing it.

Oh yeah. In the vast majoruty of time everything is good. In the vast

the GOOD judge is able to fix ANY problem, not just "majority" of
them. Even such "rare" problem as "I've lost some cards and don't

much, and these people often do "unintentional cheating".
For instance, imagine a player could use either Fear of Mekhet or
Pentex Subversion. After the first round, he discovers that he missed
one master card, though he never played it. What was the card? He
cannot remember what he put in his deck at the last moment, but he
feels that Fear of Mekhet is going to help him better at this
tournament. Surely he should take it, not Pentex! So, he puts Fear
into his deck and continues play. This can be cheating, but you don't
care - as long as you think that changing the deck between rounds
cannot bring any good :D
Should you have decklists, the problem would be resolved in a few
seconds, of course, and that player wouldn't have to cheat.

> drawing it *and then* having an opportunity to play it when it is
> gonna be useful? Very, very small.

Did I say something about sitting next? Or about it being useful or
not?
Look, if I play at the large tournament, where the stakes are high,
and somebody is playing a second Fear of Mekhet on my vampire, I'm
going to ask the judge whether he really has two Fears in his deck,
since it isn't very common. This wouldn't harm anybody, but this can
prevent the potential cheating.
Without the decklists, cheaters are welcome and well-rewarded! :D

> > 5). If you have the decklists, you can easily judge the complicated
> > PTW questions that usually require evaluation of the player's deck.
>
> Umm, you are crossing the line here from "serious judge" to "mental
> institution escapee". There are no complicated PTW questions that
> usually require evaluation of the player's deck. That is something you
> are simply making up or imagineing.

I'm not crossing anything. Just read some PTW threads here. To
determine whether the player "reasonably" can get more than, say, 1VP,
or cannot, you will need to inspect his deck (or his decklist, which
is much more convenient). I don't know what are YOU imagineing, but
it's as simple as the "untap-master-minions-influence-discard" order.
How can you make a decision without examining the deck? Oh yeah, I
know, you will just trust the player. Great.

> > 6). The claim that decklists prevent only one kind of cheating is
> > wrong.
>
> Not only does it only partially prevent one kind of cheating (i.e.
> illegal between rounds deck manipulation), it only partially prevents
> the least effective kind of cheating.

I should say this in different words. The sheet of paper cannot
prevent anything - it's just a sheet of paper. But a bunch of
decklists can HELP a good judge to prevent a lot of possible cheating.
I've demonstrated this, but why you aren't willing to see - it isn't
my problem.

>
> You realize that you, Ector, a dude who has been playing this game for
> what, maybe 2 years now, and has been running tournaments for less
> than that are standing here and decrying the ability of people who
> have been running tournaments for this game for 12 years (including
> the head game designer and guy who has run all of the North American
> Championship events) of all sizes due to your belief that not
> requiring decklists comes from a "nothing really matters to me"
> attitude? Remember that time where you were all like "Stealth and
> Bleed is dead! Bowl of Convergence kills it!" and then eventually, you
> were all like "Huh. I guess these people who have been playing this
> game competetively for a much longer time than me might know something
> I don't..."
>

Oh, too bad for me! How dare I to write that? Very simply.
A good judge is a "bastion of order". He is able to solve ANY problem
and he can restore order in the most complicated situations. Thus, a
judge that voluntarily gives up the wonderful opportunity of checking
the deck of any player (should that be necessary) and the opportunity
of helping the players to restore their decks to the original state
can NEVER be a good judge. As well as a cop that voluntarily refuses
to wield his gun can never be a good cop, even though the gun isn't
going to be needed 99% of time, and carrying it is a "hassle".
I can understand that there is a tradition of playing without the
decklists, lazyness and similar things, but this changes nothing. If
LSJ runs tournaments without the decklists, then he's probalbly not as
good judge as I supposed. He knows the rules best of all, of course,
but the judge's work isn't limited to that. I don't know whether he
feels a shame when he's unable to help the player to restore his deck
to the original status (or when he realizes that the players unable to
restore their decks are playing with the decks that differ from the
original), but I would be ashamed for sure. And the solution is very
simple: start to require the decklists at major tournaments. This will
eventually spread their usage in the whole country.
Note that I don't insist on making deckchecks prior to the finals or
at any other time. And I don't insist of issuing GLs for deck problems
at each tournament - after all, not all tournaments are as big as ECQ.
A judge may even decide to make no deckchecks at all, but the
decklists will still help a lot in maintaining order during the
tournament. And they will help BOTH the judge and the players.

Some words personally for you, Peter. IMHO, any person who can
seriously suggest dropping decklists as a "solution" for the
"draconian rule problem" cannot be a judge at all. Without the
decklists those Hungarian players would play the finals with the
illegal decks, having significant differences from the submitted
ones!!! How can a judge think that it would be better than two GLs is
completely beyond my imagination. Please think about it if you
seriously consider yourself a judge.

Yours,
Ector

> On Apr 13, 6:19 am, "Ector" <E...@mail.ru> wrote:
>
> > "Huh. What do you think is missing? Fear of Mekhet? Take two Fears,
> > there are too many ICs here!" :D
>
> You realize that hoser cards like Fear of Mekhet aren't really all
> that useful, right? Even if you illegally modify your deck to include
> them between rounds, right?

"Aren't that useful"? You must be kidding? So I'm playing the Sabbat
voting deck, and I suddently discover that there are lot of ICs at the
tournament. Not only do I risk to catch PTO, but I cannot push my
votes! Thus, I put Fear of Mekhet and dig for it. Puff! There are no
opposing votes, no PTO threat, I'm on ny road to victory.

> > Wonderful. Simply wonderful, especially at the large tournament with
> > 53 players :) Stop the whole event to find out who lost the card.
>
> You don't have to stop the whole event. You have to pause, say "Huh. I
> was sitting next to Frank last game. Lemme go ask him..."

You tend to hope for the simplest outcome. A good judge must have a
solution for ALL situations, even the most complicated. So, that
player goes to Frank, but Frank isn't sure that the HU is his. He
cannot remember for sure how many HUs he originally had, and cannot
remember the exact number of cards in his deck. Your solution? No good
solution, you are helpless. A good judge is never helpless.
This isn't even the most complicated case. You might ask all the
players at the last table "whose is the HU", and two players may want
to get it!

> > This is very, very strange. Decklists are not just a useless papers.
>
> I never claimed they were useless papers. I claimed that they don't
> actually accomplish what you hope they will most of the time, and
> aren't really worth the effort.

Decklists are the emergency tools. Failing to have them makes you
helpless in emergency situations. So, they really worth the effort as
long as you really want to have the emergency tool - which you should
want if you're a good judge. If you think that "shit never happens",
how is such attitude differ from "nothing really matters to me"?

> > LSJ really needs to start to require decklists, at least
> > at the major tournaments like Qualifiers and Nationals - and this will
> > demonstrate their value to the whole country.
>
> We've lived this long without them. I don't really think it is
> necessary to "demonstrate their value".

It's extremely strange that US players and US judges don't value such
great emergency tool as decklists. US is known as a "land of
security"... many people have guns to protect their houses, many
people report any suspicious things to the police, and so on. How can
the same country live without decklists? And why?

> > This is completely wrong. See the decklists usefulness above.
>
> You failed to convince me. Yes, they help when folks misplace cards
> (but not so much that they should be required). Yes, they
> theoretically prevent some forms of mostly ineffective cheating (but
> not so much that they should be required). Yes, they occasionally mean
> that someone is absurdly DQed from a final for a minor error.

You still confuse GL with DQ, which is not a sign of a good judge.
Really.
Decklists are just TOOLS. They don't do anything without a judge. With
a good judge, they help to prevent some cheating (not all cheating, of
course) and to maintain decks status. This is far outweights the
"hassle" of filling them.
And, Peter, the decklists don't issue any penalties. Only the judges
do. So when a judge uses the decklists to punish players too hard, he
should be blamed, not the decklists. As well as when the cop uses his
gun too aggressively, nobody even thinks about blaming the gun or
demanding to take the guns away. The judge must use his own judgement
to assign an appropriate penalty, taking into account the tournament
level, the player, the character of the infraction, and so on. BTW,
why do I have to tell you all this? Are you a judge or not?

>
> Sigh. That's right, Ector. Everyone in the US who runs big,
> competetive tournaments all the time is disorganized. 'Cause they
> don't have deck lists.

At least, they aren't organized good enough, and they definitely could
be organized better.

> > Dirty talks are the talks about "draconian rules", "too harsh
> > penalty", "effectively DQ" and so on.
>
> Getting removed from the final round of a tournament due to having one
> less card in your deck than your decklist said? That is pretty much
> draconian.

There is absolutely nothing draconian in the RULE. But it was
improperly used. Firstly, the players weren't trained enough to play
with such rules (and the judge should spend some time to explain it to
the players). Secondly, decks should be checked as soon as possible,
not only prior to the finals - at least card quantity. Should this be
done, nobody would be punished that hard - except for the potential
cheaters, against whom the rule was created.

>
> > Decklists cannot cause any "damage" at all, but they can prevent a lot of
> > tournament disruptions.
>
> Getting removed from the final round of a tournament due to having one
> less card in your deck than your decklist indicated is certainly
> damage. And more than I am willing to accept in the name of a slight
> reduction in an already very small amount of cheating.

Please read my previous answer. Rules are just tools that the judges
use to maintain order. Most of the time rules aren't "stupid" or
"draconian", but the judge should use them right.

Yours,
Ector

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <1176535444.2...@o5g2000hsb.googlegroups.com>,
"Ector" <Ec...@mail.ru> wrote:

> "Aren't that useful"? You must be kidding? So I'm playing the Sabbat
> voting deck, and I suddently discover that there are lot of ICs at the
> tournament. Not only do I risk to catch PTO, but I cannot push my
> votes! Thus, I put Fear of Mekhet and dig for it. Puff! There are no
> opposing votes, no PTO threat, I'm on ny road to victory.

That is correct. Changing your deck between rounds illegally isn't that
useful. I explained this at length in a tangental thread, but you
apparently didn't read that. In any case, yeah, let's say you discover
there are a lot of ICs in the tournament in R1. So you cheat and swap a
couple Fear of Mekhets in your deck. R2, you don't sit next to any IC
members, so you have swapped out two useful cards for two dead cards.
We'll say you are still convinced that you really want to continue
cheating for R3. And then we'll assume that you sit next to an IC member
in R3. And then we'll assume you draw a Fear in R3. You then need to be
able to play it to some effect. Have you ever actually *tried* to use
Fear of Mekhet (which is apparently the best possible example you have
for how illegally modifying your deck is a huge help)? Heck, I was main
decking two Fear of Mekhets in both of the Cultist Storyline tournaments
I played. Which weren't that huge (12-18 players) and I *knew* that
there were going to be ICs and Justicars. Ya know how many vampires got
burned by Fear of Mekhet? None. 'Cause it isn't really that good of a
card. It is highly conditional (even if you "know" there are going to be
IC members), easily foiled, risky if you are playing your own
IC/Justicars, and expensive. It is a kind of dubious hoser card that
occasionally might pay off. But most of the time, not so much. Even if
you are an unscrupulous bastard who wants to cheat and put this card in
your deck between rounds illegally.

VTES (unlike Magic) is generally not a game where single cards are going
to have such a huge impact such that cheating by sticking a few
different cards in your deck between rounds is going to have a
significant impact--you don't know who you are playing against when you
are in the process of cheating (unless you are so adept at card
manipulation that you can swap cards in and out of your deck while folks
are watching you, and if that is the case, are deck lists really gonna
stop this?); you can't guarantee that you'll be sitting anywhere near
someone who is playing a deck that is going to be affected by the cards
you put in; you can't guarantee that you'll draw the cards you put in;
you can't guarantee that the opponent you want to use those cards
against are even going to still be in the game when you do draw them,
let alone that playing them will actually do you any good.

In Magic, say, using a really old school example, if I can scout out my
next opponent somehow, discover he is playing some all white deck, and
then illegally shove 4x Brushfire (that's the one that destroys all
Plains, right?) in my deck, I'm gonna be in pretty good shape. There
isn't an analog for VTES. 'Cause you aren't playing a single opponent.
You aren't playing best 2 of 3 matches. Your deck is bigger and contains
more useful cards (i.e. 90 important that have an effect on the game as
opposed to ~40 in a 60 card deck). Illegally modifying your deck between
games in VTES just isn't that useful. If you are likely to cheat, there
are more effective ways to do it.

That, and even if putting those Fear of Mekhets were actually going to
help you out (which is assure you, is pretty unlikely in the grand
scheme), if there weren't deck lists and deck checks in play, would you,
Ector, cheat like this if you were in a tournament? I'm assuming you are
going to say "of course not". If that is the case, why are you assuming
everyone else will?

> Decklists are the emergency tools. Failing to have them makes you
> helpless in emergency situations.

What emergency situations are you imagining here, exactly? What
"emergency" is going to come up where a deck list is needed to fix it
where simple rationality and judgement can't fix it?

> It's extremely strange that US players and US judges don't value such
> great emergency tool as decklists.

For what "emergency" exactly?

> US is known as a "land of
> security"... many people have guns to protect their houses, many
> people report any suspicious things to the police, and so on.

You watch too much TV.

> How can the same country live without decklists? And why?

I can only speak for myself, really, but I'd assume that is because the
general consensus is that they aren't worth the hassle. As noted many
times in this discussion.

> You still confuse GL with DQ, which is not a sign of a good judge.

No, I don't confuse GL with DQ. In the discussion at hand, a player (two
actually) were effectively disqualified from a tournament for very minor
decklist errors. Yes. Technically, they only were given a Game Loss. But
at the point that they were given said Game Loss, it resulted in them
being removed from the finals that they rightfully got in to. So
effectively, they were disqualified from the event. I'm using DQed in
this discussion 'cause in practice, that is what happened.

> BTW, why do I have to tell you all this?

'Cause you seem to think it is important. But it really isn't.

Peter D Bakija
pd...@lightlink.com
http://www.lightlink.com/pdb6/vtes.html

> "Changing my deck between rounds is rarely going to help me"? Yes, I
> saw that utter BS, but didn't have enough time to answer it.

You have played this game, right? You have no idea who you are going to
be sitting next to, or even at the same table with, until you are
already sitting there. In your first game, you see 4 other decks. If you
die quickly and get to scout around, you might get to see another
handfull enough to have an idea of what they are doing. So you have
limited info in a limited number of decks. You can then, assuming you
are an unscrupulous bastard and want to cheat, go and put a couple of
appropriate hosers in your deck that you think might help. But then:

A) You still are pretty likely to not sit at a table that contains a
deck that you "prepped" for.

B) Even if you do sit at such a table, you are pretty likely to not be
sitting next to a deck that you "prepped" for.

C) Even if you do sit at a table with such a deck, and you sit next to
such a deck, you need to draw the card and have it actually do you some
good.

> If I noticed three decks based on ICs, putting two Fear of Mekhets
> isn't going to help me? Really?

Yes. Really. 'Cause you have to be sitting at a table with such a deck
and near such a deck and then draw the card and then be able to play it
effectively (again, have you ever actually *used* Fear of Mekhet and had
it work the way you wanted it to?). And that is just one card. Are you
going to a tournament with every card in your collection, just in case
you want to be able to dial-a-cheat?

> If I noticed a lot of weenies, Aranthebes isn't going to help me?

Not if you don't sit next to weenies in the next game. You notice a lot
of weenies in the first round. You then cheat and put in an Aranthebes.
And then the next round, you sit next to an all huge vampire deck. And
then the next round, you manage to sit next to a weenie deck, but you
don't draw the Aranthebes. How is this helping you?

> Besides, if I'm playing a combo-deck with 6 Sibyl's Tongues and 3 Drop
> Point Networks and can fetch any card in a moment, changing my "silver
> bullets" package isn't going to help me? Never read the worst crap,
> honestly.

Go ahead and play that deck and see what happens. Probably nothing that
good.

> I don't play with monkeys, since I spend some time to train them.

And here you are implying that they *would* be monkeys, except for your
magnanamous charity towards them. Man. Why do people play with you?

> But
> some of my newbies really needed time to understand what is the
> tournament, how it differs from the casual play and that they CANNOT
> change their decks during the tournament.

Hmm. Does saying "You can't change your deck during a tournament" not
suffice?

> And don't tell me that stupid people live only in Belarus :)

You seem to think that is the case, considering how you refer to your
own player base.

> You WON'T accomplish it. As long as you cannot check the decks, how
> can you be sure that the players will obey your words?

'Cause most people who play games understand that, ya know, you are
supposed to obey the rules. As that is the point of a game.

> Oh yeah. In the vast majoruty of time everything is good. In the vast
> majority of time the judge serves only as a rules guru. And so on. But
> the GOOD judge is able to fix ANY problem, not just "majority" of
> them. Even such "rare" problem as "I've lost some cards and don't
> remember which". I insist on using decklist since I always was a good
> judge in Magic, and I wish to remain a good judge in VTES.

Which if that makes you happy, go nuts. But it isn't actually necessary
for good play.

> Besides the determined cheaters, there are people who want to win too
> much, and these people often do "unintentional cheating".

If they are cheating, they are cheating. There is no such thing as
"unintentional cheating". There is either an honest mistake or someone
intentionally breaking the rules.

> I'm not crossing anything. Just read some PTW threads here. To
> determine whether the player "reasonably" can get more than, say, 1VP,
> or cannot, you will need to inspect his deck (or his decklist, which
> is much more convenient).

Again, you are inventing a problem with an invented solution--no one
will ever be in a situation where you have to look at their deck and
decide, based on the composition of their deck, if they are "playing to
win". That is utter insanity.

> Oh, too bad for me! How dare I to write that?

See, I didn't point that out just to be mean. If history has shown us
anything, it is that you, Ector, are willing to jump to conclusions
about this game based on not much actual evidence or experience. If
history has shown us anything, it is that it is *possible* that there
are folks who have a far greater depth of experience in both playing

insight that you are missing out on.

There are an awful lot of people in the world who have run an awful lot

> Thus, a

Yes, that is right. People who have been running this game for far, far,

> who was 5 minutes late to the start of round, for instance. Not that
> I'm going to do the same in VTES, but a "VP loss" would be adequate to
> maintain order, IMHO.

Wow. You'd really issue a penalty other than a formal warning to a
player who caused his table in a particular round to start 5 minutes
late? I can't think of a better way to ensure that player never came to
a tournament again; I'd be surprised if he came back to the local playgroup.

I am willing to agree with one thing: You certainly were a Magic player.
That said, you are so far off base here it's not even funny, and it's
quite scary that you somehow are surprised that people are mocking you
over this.

Ector, when a game is no longer fun, people quit playing unless there is
some other incentive. Magic tournaments quit being fun many, many years
ago, but have the incentive of large cash and/or product prizes... so
people still play. But in the last Magic tournament I saw, nobody was
having "fun"; people were throwing tantrums and literally, a chair once.
There was much yelling and arguing with the judges. That's not fun for
the players OR the judges, and nobody should waste our time pretending
that it is.

V:TES tournaments will never have that much monetary or product
incentive, so the only way to get people come to V:TES tournaments is to
make sure they have fun. Your expectation that they will somehow treat
the tournament as seriously as Magic players take their tournaments is
foolish on the face of it; there's no incentive to, nor will there ever
be. Nobody wants to alienate their friends over a few booster packs.
This, by the way, is also why there's such a blase' attitude about
cheating; it's just not worth anyone's time.

Ector, I have come to believe you have absolutely no idea what "fun" is,
and I think that's why you're having such a problem with everyone.
Perhaps there's no such thing as "officially sanctioned fun" in a
totalitarian state, and for this I feel great pity. But people have
figured out ways to have a little unofficial fun ever since the dawn of
time, and I firmly suggest that you go and find some of those people,
and talk to them about "fun" and what it is.

The only way to grow this game in _any_ country is to make sure the
people who play it have fun. Draconian punishments for the slightest
rule infraction, however, are fun for nobody, and serve only to drive
people away.

Think about it.

--
Derek

defend yourself good enough and have enough time. My Anneke deck
usually started the aggressive actions only after Temptation of

> of VTES tournaments. Heck, one year, Kevin ran, by himself, like, 12
> VTES tournaments in 3 days. And an awful lot of people who do this don't
> think that decklists and deck checks are worth the effort they take. And
> it is never a problem. You'd think that this breadth of evidence would
> support the idea that you can effectively run a tournament without
> decklists.

Those "awful lot of people" aren't taking judging tournaments
seriously enough. This may be OK for the small local tournaments, but
this cannot be tolerated at the major tournaments like Qualifiers and
Nationals. Any serious judge that really wants to run the large
tournament smoothly would require the decklists just for that purpose.
Besides, if a problem remains unnoticed that doesn't mean it didn't
happen at all. For instance, those two Hungarian players would play
the illegal decks in the finals, and that would be unnoticed without
the decklists. Not a problem for you? Then you obviously aren't a
serious judge.

> > Thus, a
> > judge that voluntarily gives up the wonderful opportunity of checking
> > the deck of any player (should that be necessary) and the opportunity
> > of helping the players to restore their decks to the original state
> > can NEVER be a good judge.
>
> Yes, that is right. People who have been running this game for far, far,
> longer than you have, and have run far, far more events that you have,
> will never be as good a judge as you, as they realize that decklists
> aren't real useful and generally noth worth the effort.

Please read the above. I'm not trying to tell that I will ever know
the rules as good as LSJ (that's impossible by definition), but as
long as I would have the decklists and LSJ wouldn't, I will be able to
maintain the better order at the tournament. And believe me, the
organized players really appreciate the order and understand that the
order is well worth filling a decklist.

>
> > Without the
> > decklists those Hungarian players would play the finals with the
> > illegal decks, having significant differences from the submitted
> > ones!!!
>
> You honestly think that having 5 Reunion Kamut instead of 6 Reunion
> Kamut is a problem worth throwing someone out of the finals of a
> tournament? Really?

I think that the problem should be discovered much earlier than after
the preliminary rounds, and I've told this at least 3 times here.
But as long as we're discussing the decklists here, it's obvious that
"throwing someone out" is better than closing your eyes on such
immense rules violation as playing the illegal deck (EVEN the deck
with 5 Reunion Kamuts instead of 6). Without the decklists that rules
violation would go unnoticed, and you seriously suggest it as a
SOLUTION!!! In this case, the proposed cure is worse than the disease.
Why "throwing somebody out" is better? Because your job as a judge is
maintaining the order, not only at this tournament, but at the ALL
tournaments you're running. If you "throw somebody out", every player
at the tournament would learn by example, and you aren't likely to
have the same problem at the next tournament. If you just close your
eyes and say: "Play with illegal decks, it doesn't matter for me" (as
you will inevitably do if you drop decklists) - you will NEVER get the
good order. For a serious judge, that is a catastrophe.
Again, I'm NOT recommending "throwing people out" prior to the finals,
but playing without the decklists and allowing people to play with
illegal decks is even worse.

> > How can a judge think that it would be better than two GLs is
> > completely beyond my imagination. Please think about it if you
> > seriously consider yourself a judge.
>
> I used to think you were funny but kind of misguided. Now I am beginning
> to think you live in a sad and creepy little world.

Actually, YOU are "funny but kind of misguided". You seem to believe
that everything should be OK, every time. No problems should arise, no
players would cheat with their decks, nobody would miss any cards from
his decks, and so on.
I live in the normal world, where there are good players, and there
are bad players; there are honest players, and there are potential
cheaters. I maintain the order to help the good and honest players to
play normally, to help the bad players to learn, and to make the
potential cheaters understand that cheating is going to be punished
pretty soon.
Believe it or not, but ALL my players appreciate my work and never
complain about the "hassle" of filling the decklists. Yes, all
players, including the potential cheaters. Even the criminals usually
respect good cops that are eager to maintain the order and despise the
cops with "nothing matters to me" attitude.

Yours,
Ector
