Messages.Body:
On Apr 15, 7:14 am, Derek Ray
<moot@idont_check_the_spamtrap_anyway.com> wrote:
Derek, I'm totally amazed to read such kind and gentle post from you!

> Wow. You'd really issue a penalty other than a formal warning to a
> player who caused his table in a particular round to start 5 minutes
> late? I can't think of a better way to ensure that player never came to
> a tournament again; I'd be surprised if he came back to the local playgroup.

A judge has to follow the rules and the recommendations. When a player
doesn't appear at the table after the pre-game time limit passes (3
minutes), a judge is recommended to issue Game Loss, which should be
upgraded to Match Loss after the next 5 minutes.
Note that it was issued at the Minsk Open Championship with 32 players
(quite big tournament for Belarus), and nobody blamed me for that GL,
as it was obviously issued according to the rules. And that player
didn't quit playing.
But I'm not going to issue anything similar in VTES, for sure...
unless somebody will be 20 minutes late without a serious reason, for
instance :)

> Ector, when a game is no longer fun, people quit playing unless there is
> some other incentive. Magic tournaments quit being fun many, many years
> ago, but have the incentive of large cash and/or product prizes... so
> people still play. But in the last Magic tournament I saw, nobody was
> having "fun"; people were throwing tantrums and literally, a chair once.
> There was much yelling and arguing with the judges. That's not fun for
> the players OR the judges, and nobody should waste our time pretending
> that it is.

You know, our Magic players DIDN'T have large cash/product prizes when
I were a judge. Most tournaments had just 2-3 boosters as a prize, not
more. We didn't have too much players to buy a lot of product, so our
support was minimal as well.
Thus, the incentive in local Magic is the same as in VTES: everyone
wants to be the best. We are having a lot of fun here - without it
people wouldn't play VTES at all, but "fun" and "order" aren't the
contradicting things. Players may joke, laugh, propose the ridiculous
deals, and so on, but this doesn't prevent them from filling the
decklists or counting their cards after each round. And yes, they also
call the judge sometimes - it's a tournament after all, and they are
playing to win, aren't they?

> V:TES tournaments will never have that much monetary or product
> incentive, so the only way to get people come to V:TES tournaments is to
> make sure they have fun. Your expectation that they will somehow treat
> the tournament as seriously as Magic players take their tournaments is
> foolish on the face of it; there's no incentive to, nor will there ever
> be. Nobody wants to alienate their friends over a few booster packs.
> This, by the way, is also why there's such a blase' attitude about
> cheating; it's just not worth anyone's time.

You may not believe, but there are people who value the victory too
much, and they can cheat even without the prize at all. Fortunately,
their number is low, but nevertheless. I didn't tell that we have a
lot of cheaters, and probably there are no determined cheaters at all,
but sometimes a player cheats almost unconsciously. I've seen several
cases.
As long as the prizes are the same in Magic and in VTES here, I cannot
see why the VTES players shouldn't take their tournaments as seriously
as Magic players. And the prize isn't everything. Our players already
see the perspective of coming to the major European events, and if you
spend $500 or more just to participate in the tournament, you are
going to take it serious for sure! Just imagine the glory of winning
the ECQ (not even talking about the EC itself) for a player from
Belarus!!!

> Ector, I have come to believe you have absolutely no idea what "fun" is,
> and I think that's why you're having such a problem with everyone.
> Perhaps there's no such thing as "officially sanctioned fun" in a
> totalitarian state, and for this I feel great pity. But people have
> figured out ways to have a little unofficial fun ever since the dawn of
> time, and I firmly suggest that you go and find some of those people,
> and talk to them about "fun" and what it is.

The "officially sanctioned fun" here is no fun at all, for sure :)
I really know what is fun, and I even joke with my players quite
often. But, again, "fun" and "order" don't contradict each other. You
can have them both. At least, I'm trying to.

> The only way to grow this game in _any_ country is to make sure the
> people who play it have fun. Draconian punishments for the slightest
> rule infraction, however, are fun for nobody, and serve only to drive
> people away.

Draconian punishments should be avoided if you can avoid them without
giving up the order.
In most cases, you can, but this require some efforts - like, as I've
mentioned, checking the decklists during round 1, calculating the
number of cards in all decks prior to round 2, and recommending the
players to count their cards after each round. There is nothing
impossible or too difficult, people just need to get accustomed to it.
This is the best solution, not dropping the decklists as somebody
suggested.
Besides, the strict order actually HELPS me to grow the game here,
since people do believe that the game isn't just a recreation, but a
serious sport. At least, some of them. I was able to convert some
Magic players to VTES - and even the best players!

Yours,
Ector

> So what? I will have just 1-2 unusable hosers in my deck. Not much of

The possible advantage is tiny. And taking the cards out of your deck
that you know are useful and replacing them with dubious hosers is more

It just isn't worth doing. Really. That, and the vast, vast majority of

is, ya know, cheating. Even without decklist rules in effect.

> Besides, at the small tournament the chances may be much higher.

less serious and decklists are less important, but large important
tournaments *need* decklists..."

> So what again? People are packing hoser cards against the most
> dangerous decks, not against the weaker ones.

So what? It isn't helping you. And if you are so worried about IC
members that you are willing to cheat to get Fear of Mekhet in your
deck, and not worried about the hoser cards being dead cards (see: "so
what" is reference to how they aren't going to be useful most of the
time), why aren't you simply using the Fear of Mekhet in your deck in
the first place?

> And this is the worst bullshit of all.

And yet it is supported by, ya know, actually playing this game, which I
kinda get the sense you don't get to do much, as you are so caught up in
the identity of "Judge" that you won't play in the tournaments that you
run.

> And I cannot understand why you don't consider the possibility of
> playing it crosstable (after all, PTO can be played crosstable,
> right?)

'Cause playing it cross table is, most of the time, going to be a stupid
thing to do.

This whole discussion is about odds. What are the odds someone is going
to actually cheat. What are the odds that someone who does cheat is
going to actually get something out of it. The cheating that you are
discussing and so desperately trying to stop (or so desperately trying
to make it look like it is worth trying to stop), i.e. illegally
shuffling hoser cards in your deck between rounds is both very unlikely
to actually happen (as most folks just aren't going to cheat like this)
and very unlikely to actually help (as the structure of the game doesn't
support it helping an awful lot). So you have two "very unlikely"s
multiplying together into what is a really, really small chance of this
sort of thing having an impact on a given tournament. Thus, why even
worry about it?

> Because they appreciate the ORDER I provide. Every good player
> appreciates the order and respects the good judge who is able to
> maintain it.

I don't know what to tell you. I can only assume you live in a land of
utter chaos, anarchy, and corruption such that people look to you as a
bastion of order in their lives. Which is bleak. But ok.

> No, I think that you don't have so much newbies as I do, and you've
> already forgot their behavior.

Uhh, even the new players I play with are, ya know, cognizant grown ups
(or at least cognizant adolescents) who can understand basic rules. And
know not to cheat.

> People tend to follow their habits, not somebody's words. Even if the
> casual player did hear your words that changing deck is prohibited
> (and you really said that), he may just forget these words after some
> rounds.

See, that you believe this is really, really sad. That, or a really
transparent ploy to prop up your argument. No one is going to "forget"
that he can't change his deck between rounds. In the span of hours.
Again, VTES players are not monkeys. Even "untrained" newbies. Even in
Belarus.

> Why you've missed my example of "unintentional cheating", then?

'Cause it was silly. There is no such thing as "unintentional cheating".
Either someone makes a legitimate mistake, which isn't a big deal, or
they intentionally cheat, which is a big deal. Intention goes a long way
in this sort of situation.

> Don't you think that such things may happen?

Not often enough that it is worth worrying about. And certainly not
often enough that it is worth kicking someone out of the finals of a
tournament for having 1 less card in his deck than his decklist says in
the name of worrying about it.

> Looks like you know little about cheating and its psychology, but
> there's nothing to doubt here, as long as you are playing without the
> decklists...

No, I know plenty about cheating. But I also know that the vast majority
of people playing this game (well, at least around here) just simply
aren't inclined to cheat. As it is stupid to cheat in a card game. And
it is especially stupid to cheat in a way that is unlikely to actually
help.

> Why didn't you search the NG as I've suggested? Here's the LSJ's words
> on this matter:

I thought LSJ wasn't as good of a judge as you thought?

> "The judge just makes a judgment as to whether the game state is
> such that 1VP is the most that that player could reasonably
> expect to get.

Sure. The game state. What is going on at the table. Not the composition

of the player's deck.

> So, what information are you going to examine if you don't need to

> look at the deck? The stars placement and various omens?

The state of the table. What the player's position is, what the player's
predator and prey's positions are, what is in play.

There will *never* be a situation where someone will need to look at
someone's decklist to determine if someone is playing to win or not.

> Those "awful lot of people" aren't taking judging tournaments
> seriously enough.

Oh, this is gonna be rich.

> This may be OK for the small local tournaments, but
> this cannot be tolerated at the major tournaments like Qualifiers and
> Nationals.

And yet it is. And it works just fine. And everyone is happy. And no one
gets thrown out of the finals due to having 1 less card in their deck
than their decklist says.

See, again, here is one of the main problems in your argument. I'm not
telling you, Ector, that you shouldn't use decklists. If you want to,
and your players are fine with it, go nuts. I'm just pointing out that
it is neither particularly necessary or useful in the grand scheme of
things. You, on the other hand, are attacking the rest of the world as
having irresponsible, sloppy, disorganized judges in the name of
propping up your argument about how they are important. That isn't
getting you anywhere. But flamed.

> Not a problem for you? Then you obviously aren't a serious judge.

Oh, Ector. You apparently have an awful lot of your sense of self
wrapped up in your identity of "serious judge". Which is kinda sad. I'm
a guy who organizes and runs tournaments. And have for a long time. When
I'm running these tournaments, I judge as necessary, organize as
necessary, and make sure folks have a good time while playing a serious
game. And never in my life have felt the need for decklists. I have
played in many, many large, "important" tournaments, none of which had
decklists, and none of which did I feel needed decklists. And they were
run by people who were doing a fine job and taking their role as judge
very seriously. And they worked fine. And no one was kicked out of the
finals for having one less card in their deck than their decklist said.
Which strikes me as a far more important goal than the opposite.

> And believe me, the
> organized players really appreciate the order and understand that the
> order is well worth filling a decklist.

I'm an organized player. I don't appreciate that filling in a decklist
is worth the order it provides.

> But as long as we're discussing the decklists here, it's obvious that
> "throwing someone out" is better than closing your eyes on such
> immense rules violation as playing the illegal deck (EVEN the deck
> with 5 Reunion Kamuts instead of 6).

I can't however see someone thinking that this sort of thing is actually

I've expected that. Realy. A "bookkeeping judge" is the most classical
example of a bad judge. He refuses to see any problems or participate
in them. He never issues penalties 'cause nothing really matters to
him besides filling a tournament report - and he often doesn't want to
hurt his relations with his playing friends. Most of the time he's
just sitting at his table or watching the game he likes. Players
quickly understand that he doesn't like questions, so they try to
solve any questions between themselves. That means that mean and
experienced players often gain the psychological advantage over the
newbies, and some of them use the advantage to increase their chances
of winning.
Compare this to the behaviour of a good judge. A good judge is always
near and always ready to answer any question and solve any problem. He
is absolutely fair, so he is going to issue any penalty recommended by
the rules, even to his closest friend. As a result, players usually
call him 10 times more than they would call a bad judge, and players
NEVER solve the complicated questions anong themselves. This
guarantees the right rulings and the fair play for all players, if the
judge isn't overcrowded. I think that a good tournament should have at
least one judge per 25-30 players, so you needed at least 4 good
judges at your Ropecon to ensure a good order.
If you don't have any open scandals at the tournament, that doesn't
mean that everything is OK. Without a good judging, this usually means
that some players perform his duties without his responsibilities.
This may (and usually does) provide them an unfair advantage. So
please don't think that having a "bookkeeper" instead of a judge is
normal.
Guess why I know the "bookkeeping" judges so well? Because we had some
of them here in Magic. I'm not playing Magic for several years, but
I'm sure that if I decided to judge the local tournament, players
would prefer me to the remaining judges, since I'm NOT a "bookkepper".
I'm a real judge, and players appreciate it.

> Rules and practical issues (like someone being late) are mostly solved
> without the judge. Players are sensible in general, which results in a
> pleasant, relaxed athmosphere (mature... old... where was I?). And
> people do play competitively here, getting angry about the game,
> personality differences and all.

If rules questions are solved without the judge, that means that the
judge is AWFUL. Or that there should be more judges. We all know that
VTES has complicated rules, and sometimes the "obvious" ruling is
completely wrong. Also, if your players tend to solve even rules
questions qithout a judge, nobody is going to notice such things as
unsportsmanlike behaviour, PTW violation, without even talking about
cheating. Don't you know that you're effectively playing without a
judge?

> I understand that the situation might be different where you play, but
> this is just to illustrate that the environment (context) corresponds
> to the perception of the role of the judge. Relaxed approach works
> well here, IMO, and as it works, I see no reason to deliberately
> increase judge's workload with mandatory decklist checking et al. The
> organising stuff is already pretty burdening, especially in large
> tournaments. And people do it for fun :)

It would be very interesting to judge your tournament and demonstrate
you how many rules violations you regularly have. You'd be really
surprised. I'm pretty sure that you wouldn't be so happy when you
would see them yourself. "Relaxed approach" really "works", if you
mean that nobody takes a gun or knife, but it never "works" in terms
of having a tournament without rules violations.
If you don't have enough judges or organising stuff, you should
recruit more. And those people should work instead of getting fun.
Somebody always works to provide fun for the rest.

Yours,
Ector

No, these are two entirely separate things.

On the one hand, you have a judge who doesn't intervene in games. This
is, by and large, a good thing. Obviously, some games will need some
intervention - correcting an incorrect play, explaining the finer points
of deal-making, or something. But most games do *not* need a judge
standing over them the whole time, because the players know how to play,
by and large.

On the other hand, you have answering questions. A judge may know a lot
about the game without necessarily wanting to intervene a lot. Or you
may get judges who think they know everything based on, I don't know,
years of experience of something irrelevant, who'll intervene all the
time.

These two things do not go hand in hand.

>Compare this to the behaviour of a good judge. A good judge is always
>near and always ready to answer any question and solve any problem.

This is fine. And this does *not* require a judge floating over every

On Apr 18, 9:53 am, James Coupe <j...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:
>
> Yet you make just as many bullshit arguments based on your Magic
> experience that you *cannot* rely on it.

Surely I cannot *rely* on it! Where did I say that I can? Obviously,
sometimes that experience even hurts, but that still doesn't mean that
it's useless.
Actually I'd say that even a football judge's experience would be
somewhat useful if that judge would decide to move to VTES. The basic
principles of judging are similar in every sport game. A good football
judge has to be near the ball to see the game as close as possible
without intervening it; he should notice all rules violations and
issue the proper penalties. As well as the good VTES judge.
BTW, does anyone think that football players are "rampant cheaters"?
No. The competition makes them to violate rules - sometimes
unintentionally, sometimes "almost unintentionally", even though you
won't find a lot of determined cheaters there. The same thing is about
VTES or any other sport game.
Note that while a football judge can become a good judge, a
"bookkeeper judge" cannot. He doesn't know the very basics, and he
doesn't want to learn. He believes that everything would be right
without him - and that's utopia. If the players don't feel that they
can call a judge EVERY MOMENT, and the judge would immediately solve
all problems, the order will disappear.

Example 1: I wasn't a judge at the local Minsk Open tournament. One
player had Rumors of Gehenna that worked for several players. When
that player was ousted, players decided (incorrectly) that Rumors
should stay on the table, since it worked for several remaining
players. Nobody even thought about calling the judge, for some
mysterious reason. It was so obvious for them! When the same situation
appeared in the finals, I was watching the game and provided a correct
ruling. Then, the players argued that the card stayed on the table in
the preliminary game!
Example 2: I was judging a tournament and noticed that a player played
Pack Alpha for Homunculus. Nobody except for me noticed that it was
illegal, since Pack Alpha allows only animals, and Homunculus isn't
animal. I'm pretty sure that the player wasn't cheating - this is
called "misrepresentation".

I can provide much more examples where the game could go (or even did
go) crazy without a good judge. His importance is so obvious that I
really cannot understand how people can refuse to see it.

> Sometimes, just sometimes, you'll get the right answer by doing the
> wrong thing. Applying Magic rulings to V:TES is the wrong thing but
> sometimes, just sometimes, you'll get answers that match. That doesn't
> mean the procedure is right, relevant, or helpful.

The rules we're discussing here are absolutely the same as the
corresponding Magic rules (more correctly, DCI rules, as they are the
same for almost all Wizards games). The games' difference cannot
change the most basic principles such as the need of issuing penalties
for illegal deck. The only different thing is the MEANING of GL in
VTES and Magic, and that's why we direly need an intermediate penalty
between Warning and GL - VP Loss would be great. But the philosophy of
these rules is the same for ALL CCGs, so I cannot see why Magic
experience cannot help here.
Any talks that VTES is "friendly" or "recreational" are just naive, as
long as the game has such rules. Should it really be non-sporting,
nobody would even think about judges or penalties. Do you need a judge
when you play Monopoly with your children?

> >So, you are trying to make me shut up, without any serious arguments,
> >but I'm trolling? I always thought that "trolling" means being rude
> >and uncivilized.
>
> No. That's not what trolling means.
>
> When someone accuses you of something and your understanding of the
> meaning does not fit the situation, it is usually sensible to look up

Thanks for your links. Sometimes things that seem obvious (such as
"troll") are not obvious at all.

"In Internet terminology, a troll is someone who intentionally posts
derogatory or otherwise inflammatory messages about sensitive topics
in an established online community such as an online discussion forum
to bait users into responding."

This is absolutely not working in my case. I don't want to "bait users
into responding" - actually, I have no time to answer the already
posted responds. If my posts were "inflammatory" - that's because
we're discussing a very important matter, and I simply have to try to
change the status quo. And the best answer to this accusation can be
found on the same page:

"The term "troll" is highly subjective. Some readers may characterize
a post as trolling, while others may regard the same post as a
legitimate contribution to the discussion, even if controversial. The
term is often used to discredit an opposing position, or its
proponent, by argument fallacy ad hominem."

I couldn't say better myself! :)
As far as I can see, "argument fallacy" is absolutely correct
statement about my opposition. They really have no arguments besides
the tradition, which is actually rather harmful.

Yours,
Ector

This number is based only on my experience. The largest VTES

> I've run nine table tournaments on my own without any trouble getting to

happen inevitably. But, certainly, I was talking just about the
"ideal" situation, i.e. ideally it would be right to have a judge per
25-30 players.

> (It also helps that I'm not afraid to yell to attract attention when
> necessary, like when starting a new round.)

Oh, that's a habit of all experienced judges. I could easily make an
announcement for a hundred of players, too :)

> >If you don't have any open scandals at the tournament, that doesn't
> >mean that everything is OK.
>
> How are you personally deciding that tournaments you're not at have so
> much disorder?

Easily. I can evaluate the number of problems that would be not solved
without my intervention. The number is quite high.

> We're not getting players coming out of the woodwork here, plying the
> newsgroup with anecdotes of "Man, there was this tournament and the
> judge was so bad, and the players were fucking each other over the
> tables, and performing satanic blood orgies, and it was crazy, and
> everything would have been better with two judges."

Surely not. But each player has its own vision of the game and its
rules, and only the judge is supposed to have the RIGHT vision. If
Noobie Tim asks the players at his table whether he can play card X o
not, the Bragging Joe will always say his opinion about it, and as
long as Tim considers him an experienced player, he won't doubt in his
words. Later, he may discover that Joe's ruling was wrong. We have
similar situations quite often.
When I told about the two judges, I meant one Head Judge and one
Assistant Judge, not two Head Judges, of course.

> >If rules questions are solved without the judge, that means that the
> >judge is AWFUL.
>
> Bullshit.
>
> Newbie: Do I get pool from the Edge in my untap phase or my master
> phase?
> Player A: Untap.
>
> Yeah, the judge is awful.
>
> Cry me a fucking river.

No need to cry at all.
Compare this to: "Hey, Judge! Do I get pool from the Edge in my untap
phase or my master phase?" This is 1000 times better, since the newbie
is absolutely sure that the judge will provide right and detailed
answer.
How can the newbie be so sure in the other players? How??? Note that
the players aren't OBLIGED to provide the right or detailed answers,
and they can provide wrong answers. How are you going to punish them
if you OCCASIONALLY get to know that they provided the wrong ruling?
They CAN really know the rules badly.
Moreover, other players can get the unwanted advantage from the
question itself. For instance: "Can I play Archon Investigation now?"
My players tend to call me, show me the card and quietly ask: "Can I
play THIS now?"
And even if sometimes the question is so simple that every more-or-
less experienced player can easily answer (as in your example),
players should get accustomed to ask a JUDGE, since answering
questions is his job. That was my point, and it's far from being
"bullshit".

> >Also, if your players tend to solve even rules
> >questions qithout a judge, nobody is going to notice such things as
> >unsportsmanlike behaviour, PTW violation, without even talking about
> >cheating. Don't you know that you're effectively playing without a
> >judge?
>
> But tournaments aren't being played without judges.

A judge that is hard to call, or a judge that doesn't oversee the
tables = no judge.

> A judge can easily make everyone aware that he/she can - and should - be
> called over if any player has any doubts about anything at all. But by
> and large, players are mature and not retards trying to subvert the
> moral fibre of society.

Yes, he can. For a "bokkeeping judge" it would be "Call me if you
cannot solve the question yourself" :)
Our players are mixed. There are mature players, and there are
newbies. All appreciate judge's attention and availability.

> I assume that in Belarus players are immature and are trying to subvert
> the moral fibre of society, based on your bizarre attitudes.

My attitude is absolutely normal.

> >It would be very interesting to judge your tournament and demonstrate
> >you how many rules violations you regularly have. You'd be really
> >surprised.
>
> Not really. As you demonstrate repeatedly, your understanding of the
> game is - erm - somewhat shaky.

Well, my experience in VTES judging isn't large enough yet. But I'm
working on it.

> Remember kids, decklists are required, no wait, recommended, no wait,
> what....?

I require the decklists for all my tournaments. And cannot see any
reasons to play without them. Even the most lazy of my players are
able to submit them.

> >"Relaxed approach" really "works", if you
> >mean that nobody takes a gun or knife,
>
> V:TES decks are not guns.
>
> You are not a policeman.
>
> Playing V:TES is not a crime.

It was just a my commentary to the word "works". How can a judge be
sure that everything is OK, if he doesn't oversee the tables?

> >but it never "works" in terms
> >of having a tournament without rules violations.
> >If you don't have enough judges or organising stuff, you should
> >recruit more.
>
> Why are you going to recruit any?

Because I feel that I won't be able to "properly serve" so many tables
alone.

> Aren't you busy getting mad that V:TES is never going to be a sport
> when, you know, it never has been one and has never pretended to be one?

To me, VTES is a sport. This madness takes no time :) All time goes to
work.

Yours,
Ector

I don't see the relevance here - are you saying it was a bad judge
because the players didn't feel the need to call him over for
something that was obvious?

You weren't a judge, but you gave a correct ruling? Did you then
disqualify all the players for arguing with you?

This game is complicated. The interactions of so many cards
frequently turn up with circumstances that players don't anticipate.
Generally, if all players think something operates in a certain way,
they're probably right.

In any event, it's always the responsibility of players harmed by
something to speak up and get the judge's input if something sounds
fishy.

These players clearly aren't taking the game seriously. You should
remind them of how seriously they should take it if they expect you to
judge them.

> Example 2: I was judging a tournament and noticed that a player played
> Pack Alpha for Homunculus. Nobody except for me noticed that it was
> illegal, since Pack Alpha allows only animals, and Homunculus isn't
> animal. I'm pretty sure that the player wasn't cheating - this is
> called "misrepresentation".

That's a game gone crazy!

It's a problem if you can't get 5 players together where either (a)
one of them knows the rules of the game or (b) is competitive enough
to challenge anything that seems wrong.

I think the reason that people here feel less of a need for judges is
that so many players remain up to date and current on the rules, for
example by reading this news group.

> I can provide much more examples where the game could go (or even did
> go) crazy without a good judge. His importance is so obvious that I
> really cannot understand how people can refuse to see it.

So those two examples were games gone crazy because they didn't have a
good judge?

Thank you. Just, thank you.

> The games' difference cannot change the most basic principles
> such as the need of issuing penalties for illegal deck.

Yes, they can. Peter gave good reasons. Dozens of times. In this
thread alone. You have to respect someone patient and willing enough
to make the exact same point over and over again without ever breaking
into condescension.

> Any talks that VTES is "friendly" or "recreational" are just naive, as
> long as the game has such rules.

The beauty of having guidelines rather than bright-line rules is that
each judge can exercise her judgment to best reflect the needs and
wants of the local player base. If the players are friendly or
recreational, they can make do with less strict rules, and enjoy
competitive game play. If your players need to feel like they are on
trial to enjoy themselves (that is why they play the game, isn't it?),
then more power to you.

> Should it really be non-sporting, nobody would even think about judges or penalties.

Or, we would have our judges spend a lot of time organizing and
coordinating the event, assigning players to tables, and resolving
rules questions as they come up.

And we use penalties to correct behavior that is significantly
detracting from the enjoyment of the game by others: penalties deter
players from ruining the good times of other players. Which is why we
keep arguing that the game is recreational.

> As far as I can see, "argument fallacy" is absolutely correct
> statement about my opposition. They really have no arguments besides
> the tradition, which is actually rather harmful.

At the core, you have no argument other than that subjectively you
think the game would be better another way. Which is fine, but is
also, you know, subjective - if your players are happy that way, more
power to you, but I hope you understand why no one else is inclined to
go along with it.

Your insistence that everyone else is wrong, rather than just leaving
it that you think it would be better, seems to be why you provoke such
a vehement response.

That and that most of your arguments make no sense, misstate others'
positions, and rely on straw men to claim absurd positions are, in
fact, reasonable.

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
Ector wrote:
> On Apr 18, 9:53 am, James Coupe <j...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:
>> Yet you make just as many bullshit arguments based on your Magic
>> experience that you *cannot* rely on it.
> Surely I cannot *rely* on it! Where did I say that I can? Obviously,
> sometimes that experience even hurts, but that still doesn't mean that
> it's useless.

Ector, the problem is that you do not know the difference.

Could M:TG experience be helpful? Possibly. Could it hurt? We know at
least two ways in which it can, since you've mentioned two mistakes
you've made where you tried to apply M:TG concepts to V:TES.

But you aren't even experienced enough to know when it'll help and when
it might hurt ... and that renders it useless.

> BTW, does anyone think that football players are "rampant cheaters"?

First, I'm going to assume that you mean round-ball football.

Second, yes, actually, diving is rampant in football, as are a number of
little pushes, shoves, knees, elbows, ... ALL outside the rules and all
of which should be called immediately. Why aren't they? The referee
cannot see because the offender is not close enough. So yes, I do think
football players are "rampant cheaters"; I just think that due to the
circumstances, both sides are permitted an equal opportunity to cheat,
so the game remains fair.

> without him - and that's utopia. If the players don't feel that they
> can call a judge EVERY MOMENT, and the judge would immediately solve
> all problems, the order will disappear.

Note that this is different from the players not _wishing_ to call the
judge because they believe they can resolve the situation on their own.

> Example 1: I wasn't a judge at the local Minsk Open tournament. One
> player had Rumors of Gehenna that worked for several players. When
> that player was ousted, players decided (incorrectly) that Rumors
> should stay on the table, since it worked for several remaining
> players. Nobody even thought about calling the judge, for some
> mysterious reason.

Because everyone was happy with the situation. As long is everyone is
playing by the same rules, even though the rules are incorrect, then the
game remains fair. No, really. Believe it, it's a fact.

> It was so obvious for them! When the same situation
> appeared in the finals, I was watching the game and provided a correct
> ruling. Then, the players argued that the card stayed on the table in
> the preliminary game!

ATROCIOUS BEHAVIOR. If you were a player in this tournament, you should
have been given a verbal warning by the judge. If you were not a
player, you should have been called aside by the judge and informed that
you were NOT a judge, and to keep your mouth shut or you would be
removed from the premises.

First and foremost, YOU COULD HAVE BEEN WRONG. Everyone makes mistakes;
since you were not a judge, it is NOT your job to make that call. While
in this case, you made a correct ruling, at some future time you might
NOT be correct, and it is NOT your place to interfere!

Second, YOU WERE NOT PLAYING THE GAME. You have no business interfering
IN ANY FASHION in a game that you are not a judge for and whose table
you are not a current, non-ousted player at. Even if the players asked
you a question about a ruling, you should CALL THE JUDGE rather than
render your own potentially-inaccurate opinion.

Ector, you have an overinflated sense of your own importance, and you
believe that your personal moral code reigns supreme over all others.
This is awful and you should rectify it immediately, for your own sake
if not for anyone else's.

> Example 2: I was judging a tournament and noticed that a player played
> Pack Alpha for Homunculus. Nobody except for me noticed that it was
> illegal, since Pack Alpha allows only animals, and Homunculus isn't
> animal.

The difference here between this and the prior example can be summed up
in three words: YOU WERE JUDGING.

Your actions here are appropriate even if you are wrong, because it is
your responsibility to make these decisions _and_ to correct illegal
play if you see it. Plus, because you are the tournament judge, you
have the right to interfere in a game in progress to do so; players who
disagree with your ruling should take it up after the game is concluded.

> I'm pretty sure that the player wasn't cheating - this is
> called "misrepresentation".

This is called "that's not even as much as a verbal warning; just tell
him 'You know that's not an animal, right?' and let them continue."

> I can provide much more examples where the game could go (or even did
> go) crazy without a good judge. His importance is so obvious that I
> really cannot understand how people can refuse to see it.

You overestimate the desire for perfect, rigid order among players.
This is a game, Ector. It will never be more than a game. You are not
capable of making it more than a game; nobody is, but certainly not you.
It will always be a game.

There will never be another Magic, or another Pokemon, or even (thank
god) another Yu-Gi-Oh. CCGs are a dying fad. People have moved on and
are doing other things now.

People want to have fun. They want to play seriously to a certain
degree, as well. But they want to have fun, first and foremost. If
everyone at a table agrees that a play is correct and you are not
present to see the incorrect play, THAT IS OK. The players are all
still happy, and are having fun. If someone is that concerned that the
'correct' ruling be made, then they will call the judge over, trust me.
I can tell you from personal experience that US players have no fear of
saying "Let's get an official ruling on that. Hey, Judge!", and I doubt
that players in Belarus are much different.

Sometimes, people will *gasp* play incorrectly, and nobody at the table
will notice. In the grand scheme of things, however, it just does not
matter. It is each player's responsibility to know the rules himself,
and to summon the judge for a ruling if he believes those rules have
been violated. If nobody summons the judge, nobody gets to complain
later "but that wasn't fair".

> same for almost all Wizards games). The games' difference cannot
> change the most basic principles such as the need of issuing penalties
> for illegal deck.

No, there really is no NEED to issue penalties for an illegal deck.
There are many circumstances where an illegal deck deserves no penalty
whatsoever, because the alteration was completely unintentional.

The classic case of a Haven Uncovered being found in someone's vote deck
is, in fact, the best example here. It is obviously not the vote
deck's. It is easy to ask the player "Who was playing Havens on you?"
and confirm with the Archon that, in fact, the player he named was at a
previous table. Then you ask the named player if his deck is intact,
and sure enough, he will say "No, I'm missing a Haven". You restore
both decks to the correct state, issue a verbal warning to "be more
careful next time", and JUST. MOVE. ON.

> The only different thing is the MEANING of GL in
> VTES and Magic, and that's why we direly need an intermediate penalty
> between Warning and GL - VP Loss would be great.

For fuck's sake, if you need an intermediate penalty between Warning and
Game Loss, then just ASSIGN ONE. Alternately, just issue a warning and
say "Next warning, for whatever reason, will be an automatic GL."

My god, are you incapable of thinking for yourself?

> But the philosophy of
> these rules is the same for ALL CCGs, so I cannot see why Magic
> experience cannot help here.

Because you are wrong. The philosophy is NOT the same.

> Any talks that VTES is "friendly" or "recreational" are just naive, as
> long as the game has such rules. Should it really be non-sporting,
> nobody would even think about judges or penalties. Do you need a judge
> when you play Monopoly with your children?

Well, Ector, it's a fact. V:TES is both friendly AND recreational.
Even the tournaments. It won't ever be anything but, no matter how much
you try to make it.

Don't like it? Better quit the game now.

> we're discussing a very important matter, and I simply have to try to
> change the status quo. And the best answer to this accusation can be
> found on the same page:

No, Ector, you do not have to change the status quo. You have to admit
that you are wrong about this, have been wrong about this, and that you
will try to learn and apply that knowledge better next time.

--
Derek

Can you please tell me what of his reasons are "good" in your eyes?
VTES is "recreational" even at ECQ level? Players never cheat? Or

something else?

> > Any talks that VTES is "friendly" or "recreational" are just naive, as

People are DIFFERENT. Strange enough that I have to tell it to you, as
you are obviously mature.
Rules about penalties are ALWAYS just guidelines, in all games, and
the judge should use his judgement. The current VTES Judge Guidelines
are minimal, and if the judge refuses to use even those, he actually
refuses to perform an important part of judge's work.
Nobody here feels that they are "on trial". But everybody knows that
the judge is near, and he isn't going to let the players cheat freely.
This really doesn't worry anybody, as we don't have the intentional
cheaters here (at least I believe so).

>

>

work, but that isn't all. Penalties were supposed to maintain the

completely sure that no cheater would spoil the "good time", for
instance - so are you suggesting to let him continue his cheating even
if you know that he cheats?
Let's imagine that one player brought a portable TV and placed it on
the table. All players are enjoying watching the TV during the game.
Will you allow that player to leave the TV on the table? I guess you

game at the sanctioned tournament? Really?

maintain order. Players are usually happy within those borders, but
they cannot cross them. Penalties for rules violation are never going
to make people happy - are you suggesting to drop them at all?
My arguments are absolutely clear. The decklists themselves don't
bring any harm, but they can provide the invaluable help in different
cases. I've already demonstrated these cases.

> Your insistence that everyone else is wrong, rather than just leaving

I know very well what does the "relaxed" atmosphere mean. No satanic
blood orgies, for sure, but no penalties for rules violation, either.
Some rules violations would inevitably remain unnoticed, some rulings
provided by the players will inevitably appear to be wrong. As long as
I'm a judge, I cannot tolerate such things, and I'm obliged to do my
best to prevent them. Very simple, right?

>That and that most of your arguments make no sense, misstate others' positions, and rely on straw men to claim >absurd positions are, in fact, reasonable.

Your accusations are ridiculous. If you don't see the sense in my
arguments that doesn't mean that they make no sense. As well, the word
"absurd" adds nothing to the discussion - everybody just keeps his
opinion. If I cannot understand someone's point of view that isn't a
crime. What "straw men" I was relying on?

Yours,
Ector

> > BTW, does anyone think that football players are "rampant cheaters"?
>
> First, I'm going to assume that you mean round-ball football.
>
> Second, yes, actually, diving is rampant in football, as are a number of
> little pushes, shoves, knees, elbows, ... ALL outside the rules and all
> of which should be called immediately. Why aren't they? The referee
> cannot see because the offender is not close enough. So yes, I do think
> football players are "rampant cheaters"; I just think that due to the
> circumstances, both sides are permitted an equal opportunity to cheat,
> so the game remains fair.

No football judge would agree with such opinion. Players are supposed
to play fair, and they are severely punished for violation of rules.
Sorry, but "permitted an equal opportunity to cheat" sounds just
crazy. Are you going to say that the penalized players just exceeded
that "allowed" opportunity to cheat?
More importantly: why do you think that VTES players don't have "equal
opportunity to cheat", too? This game also has its "little pushes,
shoves, knees and elbows". You may look at the other player's hand,
intentionally or not, you may "unintentionally" draw an extra card
(and then put it back), and so on.

> > without him - and that's utopia. If the players don't feel that they
> > can call a judge EVERY MOMENT, and the judge would immediately solve
> > all problems, the order will disappear.
>
> Note that this is different from the players not _wishing_ to call the
> judge because they believe they can resolve the situation on their own.

Yes, it's different. A judge should encourage players to ask him
questions, not to "resolve on their own". If the players don't wish to
call a judge, the judge should investigate why (after the tournament,
of course). Maybe, he was too far away, or he was too busy? Maybe some
people don't respect his knowledge? This is a serious problem for a
person who wants to become a good judge.

> > Example 1: I wasn't a judge at the local Minsk Open tournament. One
> > player had Rumors of Gehenna that worked for several players. When
> > that player was ousted, players decided (incorrectly) that Rumors
> > should stay on the table, since it worked for several remaining
> > players. Nobody even thought about calling the judge, for some
> > mysterious reason.
>
> Because everyone was happy with the situation. As long is everyone is
> playing by the same rules, even though the rules are incorrect, then the
> game remains fair. No, really. Believe it, it's a fact.

LSJ, are you reading this??? Do you think that it's normal and can be
tolerated, too?
I'm totally shocked with this. Any player that do everything, as long
as he can convince the table to be happy :)

> > It was so obvious for them! When the same situation
> > appeared in the finals, I was watching the game and provided a correct
> > ruling. Then, the players argued that the card stayed on the table in
> > the preliminary game!
>
> ATROCIOUS BEHAVIOR. If you were a player in this tournament, you should
> have been given a verbal warning by the judge. If you were not a
> player, you should have been called aside by the judge and informed that
> you were NOT a judge, and to keep your mouth shut or you would be
> removed from the premises.
>
> First and foremost, YOU COULD HAVE BEEN WRONG. Everyone makes mistakes;
> since you were not a judge, it is NOT your job to make that call. While
> in this case, you made a correct ruling, at some future time you might
> NOT be correct, and it is NOT your place to interfere!
>
> Second, YOU WERE NOT PLAYING THE GAME. You have no business interfering
> IN ANY FASHION in a game that you are not a judge for and whose table
> you are not a current, non-ousted player at. Even if the players asked
> you a question about a ruling, you should CALL THE JUDGE rather than
> render your own potentially-inaccurate opinion.

You are completely right with all your points here. I should add that
the judge couldn't provide the exact ruling and asked the players to
share their points of view. But nevertheless, here you see just
another good example of the importance of good judge.

> Ector, you have an overinflated sense of your own importance, and you
> believe that your personal moral code reigns supreme over all others.
> This is awful and you should rectify it immediately, for your own sake
> if not for anyone else's.

I hate to say it, but you're absolutely right here. Still, I'd prefer
a judge with similar problems to the judge that doesn't care much
about anything. At least, I do have a strict moral code.

> > Example 2: I was judging a tournament and noticed that a player played
> > Pack Alpha for Homunculus. Nobody except for me noticed that it was
> > illegal, since Pack Alpha allows only animals, and Homunculus isn't
> > animal.
>
> The difference here between this and the prior example can be summed up
> in three words: YOU WERE JUDGING.
>
> Your actions here are appropriate even if you are wrong, because it is
> your responsibility to make these decisions _and_ to correct illegal
> play if you see it. Plus, because you are the tournament judge, you
> have the right to interfere in a game in progress to do so; players who
> disagree with your ruling should take it up after the game is concluded.

No, this is wrong way for a discussion. I can provide you some
examples of my utter mistakes, if you wish :) These examples were
posted to demonstrate the importance of a good judge, and please don't
think that I consider myself a good judge in VTES right now - but I
know what a good judge needs, and I'm going to become it.

> > I'm pretty sure that the player wasn't cheating - this is
> > called "misrepresentation".
>
> This is called "that's not even as much as a verbal warning; just tell
> him 'You know that's not an animal, right?' and let them continue."

I did right that. Again, the example was posted to demonstrate that
such violation of rules could go unnoticed without the judge. Any
judge can notice some mistakes of this kind if he's going to observe
the games.

>
> You overestimate the desire for perfect, rigid order among players.
> This is a game, Ector. It will never be more than a game. You are not
> capable of making it more than a game; nobody is, but certainly not you.
> It will always be a game.
>
> There will never be another Magic, or another Pokemon, or even (thank
> god) another Yu-Gi-Oh. CCGs are a dying fad. People have moved on and
> are doing other things now.

>From my perspective, CCGs are still very popular, and their popularity
is only increasing here.
And I really can't stand such words as "it's only a game". It's a
GAME!!! You could say "It's only a life". Spending your time at the
things that doesn't really matter to you isn't very clever. So,
players that don't take the game seriously are going to leave, but the
rest players will remain.

> People want to have fun. They want to play seriously to a certain
> degree, as well. But they want to have fun, first and foremost. If
> everyone at a table agrees that a play is correct and you are not
> present to see the incorrect play, THAT IS OK. The players are all
> still happy, and are having fun.

People want to *win*, first and foremost. If they don't, they are
playing different game, not VTES, since VTES players must play to win.
Having fun is great, as long as it doesn't prevent you from playing to
win.

> If someone is that concerned that the
> 'correct' ruling be made, then they will call the judge over, trust me.
> I can tell you from personal experience that US players have no fear of
> saying "Let's get an official ruling on that. Hey, Judge!", and I doubt
> that players in Belarus are much different.

Yes, they can call a judge, if they feel that the judge is ready and
willing to answer the questions. A "bookkeeper judge" isn't usually
happy with questions, so the players rarely ask them. That's the
difference I tried to demonstrate.

> Sometimes, people will *gasp* play incorrectly, and nobody at the table
> will notice. In the grand scheme of things, however, it just does not
> matter. It is each player's responsibility to know the rules himself,
> and to summon the judge for a ruling if he believes those rules have
> been violated. If nobody summons the judge, nobody gets to complain
> later "but that wasn't fair".

This is false, which was demonstrated by LSJ himself when we discussed
"correcting the game state". If you noticed that your vampire was
improperly burned a turn ago, you still can call a judge, and the
judge would have to correct the game state according to his judgement.

> > same for almost all Wizards games). The games' difference cannot
> > change the most basic principles such as the need of issuing penalties
> > for illegal deck.
>
> No, there really is no NEED to issue penalties for an illegal deck.
> There are many circumstances where an illegal deck deserves no penalty
> whatsoever, because the alteration was completely unintentional.
>
> The classic case of a Haven Uncovered being found in someone's vote deck
> is, in fact, the best example here. It is obviously not the vote
> deck's. It is easy to ask the player "Who was playing Havens on you?"
> and confirm with the Archon that, in fact, the player he named was at a
> previous table. Then you ask the named player if his deck is intact,
> and sure enough, he will say "No, I'm missing a Haven". You restore
> both decks to the correct state, issue a verbal warning to "be more
> careful next time", and JUST. MOVE. ON.

Yes, this is a decent way to resolve the problem if the HU was
discovered between rounds. I never said that a player deserves a
penalty for leaving HU. But every player is responsible for STARTING
EACH ROUND with the same deck. What are you going to do if that voting
deck player DRAW that HU during the game, for instance? Rules were
meant to make the players disciplined and avoid such things whenever
possible.
But the current penalty for illegal deck is too harsh, without any
questions, since GL is a very big penalty for VTES. That can force
some judges to avoid deckckecks at all. We really need Dave's "VP
Loss" and the new Judges Guidelines.

> > The only different thing is the MEANING of GL in
> > VTES and Magic, and that's why we direly need an intermediate penalty
> > between Warning and GL - VP Loss would be great.
>
> For fuck's sake, if you need an intermediate penalty between Warning and
> Game Loss, then just ASSIGN ONE. Alternately, just issue a warning and
> say "Next warning, for whatever reason, will be an automatic GL."

I do this regularly. But issuing penalties without any guidelines is
too much responsibility for a single man, IMHO. People shouldn't be
punished without the law.

> My god, are you incapable of thinking for yourself?

I always have my opinion. But it's just my opinion, not the sanctioned
recommendation, and I need the LAW. Without the proper law, players
are free to complain about the penalties being "too harsh" or "too
weak". And the law should be logical, without issuing GL for illegal
deck.

> > But the philosophy of
> > these rules is the same for ALL CCGs, so I cannot see why Magic
> > experience cannot help here.
>
> Because you are wrong. The philosophy is NOT the same.

At least it's explained in the same words. Why should it be different,
then?

> > Any talks that VTES is "friendly" or "recreational" are just naive, as
> > long as the game has such rules. Should it really be non-sporting,
> > nobody would even think about judges or penalties. Do you need a judge
> > when you play Monopoly with your children?
>
> Well, Ector, it's a fact. V:TES is both friendly AND recreational.
> Even the tournaments. It won't ever be anything but, no matter how much
> you try to make it.
>
> Don't like it? Better quit the game now.

Our tournaments aren't "recreational" for sure. Players get really
tired after them. And even if the tournaments are "friendly", that
doesn't mean that tournaments are not sport events here. No need to
quit the game for me.

> > we're discussing a very important matter, and I simply have to try to
> > change the status quo. And the best answer to this accusation can be
> > found on the same page:
>
> No, Ector, you do not have to change the status quo. You have to admit
> that you are wrong about this, have been wrong about this, and that you
> will try to learn and apply that knowledge better next time.

I'd sooner quit the game than admit that I'm wrong about this. Really.
You have your own way and pretend that it's the best way - me too. I
don't think that my disciplined players will have any problems at the
foreign tournaments, and I don't think that foreign players are going
to have any serious problems here: as long as I'm aware that some
playgroups are badly organized, I can warn foreign players at the
beginning of the tournament.

Yours,
Ector

I think you generate a lot of preconceived notions and fantasies about this

to pull whatever value I can from your posts, wrt your Magic background.

that is) and you're not giving me anything more.

but moreso, I don't understand why you fail to see that many interpret your
level of intervention and highly servere penalties as "activist judging".

ON the other side of the cheating coin, who is to say that an overly

>

Once again, you are extrapolating from your personal experience onto the
rest of the international player base, and not even realizing how your own
attitude towards judging reinforces a bias towards more Judge involvement,
not less... Cripes, if I knew the sort of penalties you apply for players
resolving rules issues for themselves, I'd be calling you over five times a
game, too, if only for fear of you slinging a GL at me for trying to
resolve it myself. You've fostered the specific environment of your own
tournaments, and it seems you have no direct experience with any
alternatives. I hope you have the chance to see how others treat the VTES
tournament scene some day. The lack of anarchy, fistfights, and gunfire
will amaze you.

>> We're not getting players coming out of the woodwork here, plying the

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <1176933284....@d57g2000hsg.googlegroups.com>,
Ector <Ec...@mail.ru> wrote:

> Fine. If everything is OK, the judge wouldn't mess. But is everything
> ALWAYS goes right? I'd say that a bad judge just refuses to see any
> problems. And that's awful.

And again, no one has ever claimed that there are never any problems.
Are you familiar with the term "Straw Man"? That is when you make up a
point to argue against that none of your opponents have actually made,
just to strengthen your argument. This here is what we like to call a
"Straw Man". No one has ever claimed that there are *never* any problems
and that Judges don't occasionally need to fix stuff. There are
occasionally problems, and Judges sometimes need to fix stuff--rules
questions that no one can come to a consensus on, situations where there
is a mess due to someone missing something and having the rewind the
game a few steps, the occasional question/situation involving possible
collusion and/or playing to win, whatever. In my experience, (and
likely the experience of most of the folks on this here newsgroup) is
that this is Judges do most of the time--they step in where needed or
asked, fix things that need fixing, but otherwise, let the players do
what they need to do. Which works fine as, again, most folks who play
this game competetively are smart, reasonable folks who can fix minor
errors and rules questions on their own and neither need a judge at
their every beck and call or hovering over their game constantly.

Again, where this interacts with decklists and all, is that the vast
majority of the time, there is nothing that goes wrong that a decklist
is needed to fix. Yes, you are correct that in the grand scheme, filling
out decklists aren't a huge imposition (although they certainly will
contribute to turnning some folks off tournaments), and if they aren't
being used to DQ folks at the last second due to missing a single card,
they can't really hurt anything. But much like having a judge hovering
over every table all the time, they tend to cross the line into "not
really necessary to do a good job as a judge".

> The more questions your players will ask, the better judge you are.

That is a strange comment. I'd never claim that people shouldn't ask
questions--when I am judging an event, that is why I am there, and there
are regularly folks shouting weird questions across the room. But I'd
never equate "people asking me questions" with "being a good judge". But
ok.

> This number is based only on my experience. The largest VTES
> tournament I've run had 21 players, and it was extremely difficult to
> run it. I seriously doubt that I will be able to answer all questions
> of 40 players and oversee 8 tables at once.

Why was it difficult to run a 21 player tournament? What was difficult
about it? I have run tournaments that big (although not much bigger),
and other than getting everyone sitting down at their tables and ready
to go (as it is like herding cats), nothing was remotely difficult about
it.

> Well, things may seem to run smoothly, but, IMHO, if ANY player
> refused to call a judge and decided to get an answer from the other
> players on his table - that's very bad and can lead to serious
> misrepresentations and violations of rules.

Why? How is that going to lead to "misrepresentation"? You are sitting
at a table with 4 other people. If you have a rules question, you ask
the table. Someone probably knows the answer. Multiple people probably
know the answer. Someone will likely give you the right answer. If there
is a question as to the validity of the answer, *then* you call the
judge.

Player A: "When do I get pool for keeping the edge?"
Player B: "Untap."
Player C: "Correct."

Everyone moves on.

Player A: " Can I play Majesty after you have Immortally Grappled me?"
Player B: "Nope. Only hand strikes."
Player A: "Are you sure?"
Player B: "That's what is says on the card."
Player C: "That's true."
Player A: "I'm gonna ask the judge."
Player B: "No problem."

And everyone moves on.

This isn't "refusing to call the judge". This is "playing a game with a
lot of people sitting around you who probably know the rules".

> How can the newbie be so sure in the other players? How???

Ah, yes, I forgot. You apparently live in a land of rampant corruption
and lies. Where everyone is more likely to stab their own mother in the
face if no one is watching than not.

Again, the vast majority of the time, folks playing this game are going
to be:

A) Honest.
B) Totally on the up and up.
C) Probably correct about the rules.

Even when playing in the finals of a large qualifier tournament. The
vast majority of the time, if someone asks the table a rules question,
they are going to get the correct answer from the table. And in the
small number of instances where there is dispute or confusion, there is
still a judge to fix things.

> Note that the players aren't OBLIGED to provide the right or detailed answers,
> and they can provide wrong answers.

No, they aren't obliged to provide right or detailed answers. But the
vast majority of the time, they will. 'Cause most people playing this
game aren't, ya know, total dicks. Lying about the rules is stupid. Just
like cheating is stupid. Most folks playing this game, when asked a
rules question will give out the correct answer to the best of their
knowlege. And if there is still ambiguity or someone isn't sure, or
folks have a dispute, the judge can fix everything.

> My attitude is absolutely normal.

It is normal to assume that everyone is a lying, cheating bastard who
constantly needs oversight and threats of punishment to not act in a
reprehensible manner? That is pretty bleak, man.

> It was just a my commentary to the word "works". How can a judge be
> sure that everything is OK, if he doesn't oversee the tables?

He can be reasonably confident that everything is ok without constant
oversight. And in the end, when everyone has a good time and nothing
horrible happens, he can continue to be reasonably confident that
everything was ok.

Messages.Body:

> What "straw men" I was relying on?

I'll point them out in this post. Refer to Peter Bakija's helpful
definition for further understanding.

> That's the whole point!!! Players often make such mistakes, ALL of
> them, even the most experienced ones that regularly read this NG. See

> completely sure that no cheater would spoil the "good time", for

> I feel like I'm talking with drug addicts or hippies!

Not a straw man, but hilarious. I hear this being said in Sgt. Joe

> Is "making your players happy" your only goal?

4) Straw man.

No one is arguing that this is a judge's only goal. You made that

> People can be happy with very different
> things. If some of your players think that changing some rules would

Messages.Author: crispyfloss
Messages.Body:
On Apr 19, 3:22 am, Ector <E...@mail.ru> wrote:
> On Apr 19, 1:23 am, crispyfloss <crispyfl...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > I don't see the relevance here - are you saying it was a bad judge
> > because the players didn't feel the need to call him over for
> > something that was obvious?
>
> No. It was a bad judge just because he wasn't near the table at the
> moment. Should he were near and be ready to answer, players would
> definitely ask him. And while it may be obvious to you, it doesn't
> have to obvious to your players.

In my experience, no one has ever been deterred from asking a judge a
question because the judge wasn't near by. In larger games, spread
out across multiple rooms in a venue, we've paused a game for the 2 or
3 minutes it takes for someone to go find a judge to bring them back
to ask a question. This hasn't ever been a problem.

I wouldn't rush to blame it on the judge in this case. After all, if
he was near this table, wasn't he necessarily far from another table,
which would then not have a judge near it?

> > This game is complicated. The interactions of so many cards
> > frequently turn up with circumstances that players don't anticipate.
> > Generally, if all players think something operates in a certain way,
> > they're probably right.
>
> I've provided two examples when they were WRONG, and now you are
> telling me the opposite.

In the first case, it was a judge that was wrong, so that's not
responsive to my point. If you were a player, and a judge issued a
ruling that you knew was wrong, you would have to abide by it.

> For instance, Peter D. Bakija himself was mistakingly thinking that
> Skin of Night can prevent Rotschreck - you can safely assume that
> the less experienced players at his table going to believe his rulings.

Regardless of who says it, If he's the one playing Rotschreck, I would
be inclined to believe him, because he's saying something that harms
him.

If he's the one playing Skin of Night, then I wouldn't disbelieve him,
but I'd want a judge to verify it because he's saying something that
is beneficial to him.

So I'd call a judge over.

Ironically, a less experienced player would probably trust a ruling by
someone like Peter less than a more experienced player, since a more
experienced player knows more of his reputation and has had more
opportunities to see him exercise his judgment first hand.

> If any player isn't completely sure about some ruling, he can call the
> judge if the judge is near. This never hurts. If the judge isn't near,
> the player isn't going to look for him. Simply enough.

This is the problem that everyone keeps referring to. As far as I can
tell this discussion started as something like:

Organizing, hands-off judges are horrible and watchful, hands-on
judges are great.

If you qualified this at the beginning with "Our players don't ask
questions, so we need to keep an eye on them to make sure you're
playing right," then everyone would understand where you're coming
from. It's that you assume that everyone knows this, and then make
statements that say you think it's true of everyone. Which, I think
understandably, rubs people the wrong way.

> Any player can make a mistake about rules. Even the most serious one.

Even a judge. And 5 good players will tend to give a better answer
than 1 good judge.

> > I think the reason that people here feel less of a need for judges is
> > that so many players remain up to date and current on the rules, for
> > example by reading this news group.
>
> That's the whole point!!! Players often make such mistakes, ALL of
> them, even the most experienced ones that regularly read this NG. See
> Peter's example above. Playing the game takes a lot of efforts and
> nerves, so even the most experienced players can do the stupid
> mistakes. Pretending that all players (or even most players) know the
> rules well enough to make such cases impossible is just naive!

And the reason some of us don't agree with what you say is that all
judges are players, and prone to the same mistakes.

Pretending that a judge knows the rules well enough to make such cases
impossible is just as naive.

Except, here's the thing: if you ask 5 players, the odds of a careless
mistake goes down. The odds of seeing the right answer goes up. If
you ask one judge, the odds of a careless mistake increases. Since
careless mistakes are hard to see when you make them yourself.

> Can you please tell me what of his reasons are "good" in your eyes?
> VTES is "recreational" even at ECQ level? Players never cheat? Or
> cheating with your deck isn't going to bring you any advantages? Or
> something else?

Cheating in this way doesn't give substantial advantages because it is
a multiple-player game.
The penalty is more likely to punish the innocent than the guilty.
Individual cards simply aren't that powerful.
Just accept this is an area where we disagree.

>
> > > Any talks that VTES is "friendly" or "recreational" are just naive, as
> > > long as the game has such rules.
>

> >....

>
> Rules about penalties are ALWAYS just guidelines, in all games, and
> the judge should use his judgement. The current VTES Judge Guidelines
> are minimal, and if the judge refuses to use even those, he actually
> refuses to perform an important part of judge's work.
> Nobody here feels that they are "on trial". But everybody knows that
> the judge is near, and he isn't going to let the players cheat freely.
> This really doesn't worry anybody, as we don't have the intentional
> cheaters here (at least I believe so).

That is what our judges do, too. Without deck lists.

> > And we use penalties to correct behavior that is significantly
> > detracting from the enjoyment of the game by others: penalties deter
> > players from ruining the good times of other players. Which is why we
> > keep arguing that the game is recreational.
>
> Organizing and coordinating the event is the important part of judge's
> work, but that isn't all. Penalties were supposed to maintain the
> "fair play", NOT to maintain the "good times of players". I'm
> completely sure that no cheater would spoil the "good time", for
> instance - so are you suggesting to let him continue his cheating even
> if you know that he cheats?

Any cheater would spoil the good times of players, because players
come to play a game with certain rules. They deliberately agree not
to do certain things, because not doing those things lets them show
how good they are at playing. Finding out that another player is
doing exactly that ruins the good time.

Even as recreation.

Fair play makes the game fun.

People don't play games to win - they play to win according to rules
they agree to with other players.

> I feel like I'm talking with drug addicts or hippies! Is "making your
> players happy" your only goal?

Not the only goal, but a very important one. If people don't enjoy
the playing the game, they won't play any more. The game is better
the more players are in it, because it makes more interactions.
Players enjoy the game because of the challenge. Players agree that
the rules of the game are the best way to have that fun.

> People can be happy with very different things. If some of your players
> think that changing some rules would make them happier, you are going
> to allow them to play the different game at the sanctioned tournament?
> Really?

No - but I might have a sanctioned tournament for the people that like
the rules how they are, and an unsanctioned tournament for people that
wanted to play by different rules. So that everyone can play and have
a good time.

> Players must obey the rules, judges must enforce the rules and
> maintain order. Players are usually happy within those borders, but
> they cannot cross them. Penalties for rules violation are never going
> to make people happy - are you suggesting to drop them at all?

A penalty for a rules violation will make all the players that are
following the rules happy. That's most of the players.

And if a good, honest player that had done very well in original
rounds had an extra Reunion Kamut in his deck or was missing a Secure
Haven in his deck, and was disqualified from the finals on that basis,
that would probably make more players unhappy than it made happy.

Because that's seen as being unfair.

If in your group, people think that's fair, and want to catch those
players, because otherwise they think they're being treated unfairly
and therefore not having fun, then use decklists. Catch them. Punish
them. But realize that we differ here, because it's what the players
want.

> I know very well what does the "relaxed" atmosphere mean. No satanic
> blood orgies, for sure, but no penalties for rules violation, either.

Then you don't understand what we mean when we say "relaxed
atmosphere." Because appropriate penalties for rules violations are
the norm. We disagree on what's appropriate, but again, that's not
disagreeing with the rules. Just how much punishment is appropriate,
and therefore how much effort should be put into finding violations.

> Some rules violations would inevitably remain unnoticed, some rulings
> provided by the players will inevitably appear to be wrong. As long as
> I'm a judge, I cannot tolerate such things, and I'm obliged to do my
> best to prevent them. Very simple, right?

If you cannot tolerate such things.

If your players want you to not tolerate such things.

Then yes.

If the players thing that's all ridiculous, then it would make sense
to not do them, right? As long as you were still following the
rules? Which give you all kinds of discretion about how to do things?

You don't have to justify your discretion to anyone here, you have to
justify it to your players. It's why it's called discretion.

Note also that the official tournament rules pretty explicitly allow for
the fact that a judge won't necessarily be available immediately -
lengthy rulings allow extra time, and the multi-judge system means that
all judges will be busy when a ruling is needed. So you pause for a
moment and move on.

e.g. judges 1 and 2 might be in the middle of a complicated combat on
another table, so you let them finish it before coming to give a ruling
on another table. Particularly "troublesome"[0] in small tournaments,
perhaps, where several judges may be tied up on one table.

[0] In as much as responsible adults waiting a minute for a judge to
finish a tricky play is ever "trouble".
