Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
On Apr 19, 4:34 pm, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>
> I think you generate a lot of preconceived notions and fantasies about this
> topic, mostly in an attempt to justify what appears to be a very heavy
> handed application of penalties, by VTES standards. I'm really trying hard
> to pull whatever value I can from your posts, wrt your Magic background.
> Nothing has come up since the little historical nugget about the relative
> strengths of Game Loss in the original Duelist Convocation rules. I'm
> trying hard, here, Ector, reading everything you've written (painful as
> that is) and you're not giving me anything more.
> I largely don't see the need for such a hard-line approach to judging,
> but moreso, I don't understand why you fail to see that many interpret your
> level of intervention and highly servere penalties as "activist judging".

OK, let's make some things clear.
1). I agree that issuing GL for illegal deck is too harsh for most
VTES tournaments. I told that from the very beginning. Your "VP Loss"
would be a perfect penalty for such infraction. But for the ECQ, this
penalty may be OK. In That Other Game judges were recommended to issue
Match Loss for this infraction, and it's roughly the same as GL in
VTES. Note that current DCI recommendations advice GL for all RELs, so
we can easily consider it too harsh EVEN for ECQ. But as long as the
current VEKN Judge Guidelines recommend GL, nobody cannot accuse the
judge that followed that recommendation. We obviously need the new
Guidelines.
2). I DON'T recommend issuing heavy penalties in any cases. Actually,
I think that the judge should try to *prevent* any rules violations -
it's easier to prevent a disease than to cure it. Did you notice my
recommendations for avoiding issuing GLs in the finals?
3). I think that decklists never hurt, but can help sometimes. Thus,
playing without them isn't very clever in any case. But suggesting to
drop them as a way to avoid issuing GLs for illegal deck is a pure
insanity! Judge can avoid issuing penalties that are too harsh even
with decklists.
4). I don't believe that the judge can really rely on things like
"players are friendly", "players know the rules" or something similar.
In many cases, this appears to be wrong.
5). I cannot agree that VTES isn't a sport game, at least at high-
level tournaments like ECQ, EC and Nationals. You may call this a
bias, if you wish.

Aren't most of my statements normal enough? Yes, I was drawn into the
stupid discussion here, so most of my posts weren't much helpful. But
that doesn't mean that I cannot produce any help, for sure.

> ON the other side of the cheating coin, who is to say that an overly
> prosecutorial judge (not you, specifically) isn't doing so to somehow
> benefit certain players within the field? One has to be cautious with an
> "I Am the Law" attitude, it'll bite them in the ass the first time a player
> thinks the Judge might be applying a too-intense penalty for out of game
> considerations...

My "I Am the Law" attitude always means that I'm trying to maintain
order, but not with the harsh penalties, if I can avoid them. That
doesn't mean that I'm not going to issue these penalties if I have to,
but that certainly doesn't mean that rules violations are nothing to
me. Please compare:

a). Hippie approach: "Players never cheat". Or at least "I have no
chances of prevent cheating, so I won't bother".
b). Maniac prosecutor approach: "Aha! You were cheating! DQ!!!"
c). My approach: "Attention everybody! Please be VERY careful with
your decklists. Check them twice prior to submitting them. Also, check
the number of cards in your deck after each round. You may get GL for
illegal deck, so let's avoid that, OK?" Add the quick card numbers
check that I've recommended, and the chances of GL are seriously
reduced. Yes, I may HAVE to issue GL even after that, and, obviously,
I won't be happy doing that.

Hope that difference is clear enough.

> > The more questions your players will ask, the better judge you are. My
> > players don't hesitate to ask even the most newbish and the most
> > obvious questions if they aren't sure.
>
> In what way do you think matters are _any_ different, if a less severe
> attitude is taken by the Judge wrt penalty magnitude?

I just wanted to show that "hippie" approach to the judging (or
"bookkeeper" approach, if you wish) inevitably leads to the decrease
of the judge's support of the players. As long as the judge thinks
that players are good and they can play without him, this is
inevitable. As long as the judge doesn't demonstrate that he's willing
to investigate the possible cheating/unsportsmanlike behaviour and
issue the proper penalties, players won't even report the suspicial
cases to him. And so on.

> > Well, things may seem to run smoothly, but, IMHO, if ANY player
> > refused to call a judge and decided to get an answer from the other
> > players on his table - that's very bad and can lead to serious
> > misrepresentations and violations of rules.
>
> Depends very much on the players involved, and whether an atmosphere of
> good will has been fostered. Usually, a pair of experienced players
> resolving a game play issue through the applicaiton of logic can arrive at
> a reasonable answer themselves, and appeal to a judge if a satisfactory
> answer for all is not found.

Players may provide a wrong ruling, and be sure that the ruling is
correct. This happens very often, even with the good and experienced
players. A judge is supposed to know the rules very well. So, he
should encourage the players to ask him, not the other players.

>
> Once again, you are extrapolating from your personal experience onto the
> rest of the international player base, and not even realizing how your own
> attitude towards judging reinforces a bias towards more Judge involvement,
> not less... Cripes, if I knew the sort of penalties you apply for players
> resolving rules issues for themselves, I'd be calling you over five times a
> game, too, if only for fear of you slinging a GL at me for trying to
> resolve it myself. You've fostered the specific environment of your own
> tournaments, and it seems you have no direct experience with any
> alternatives. I hope you have the chance to see how others treat the VTES
> tournament scene some day. The lack of anarchy, fistfights, and gunfire
> will amaze you.

Why do you think that I'm issuing any penalties to players for
resolving rules issues for themselves? There are no recommended
penalties for that, and I don't invent the rules, I just follow them.
No penalties for that, for sure, but I constantly tell my players to
ask me, not the other players. And they really ask me - why not?

>
> WHat do the other 3 players at the table do when Braggin Joe drops a wrong
> ruling? In not-Belarus, any exploitation of rules questions to a player's
> advantage over a newbie should be obvious to the others at the table, and
> then a Judge would be called over.

In most cases, the other 3 players (or 2 players at the 4-players
table) are just not sure enough to say that Joe's ruling is wrong. Or
it just doesn't matter to them. Do you remember the example with
Rumors of Gehenna?

> > How can the newbie be so sure in the other players? How???
>
> Its a five player game. If any one offers a wrong answer (to exploit the
> situation) the other three will call him on it...

Again, they MAY call. They may fail to recall the proper ruling, they
may think about the different things at the moment, they may don't
care about teaching the newbies, and so on.
Note that even if somebody call a judge, and the judge will find out
that the ruling was incorrect, that won't be enough to accuse that
player in cheating, right?

> Meh. Its a weak point. Nearly all new players will recognize situations
> where they do not want the table to have information about the contents of
> their hand prior to obtaining a ruling.

Though weak, it's still a point. Believe me, some newbies regularly
fail to recognize such situations.

>
> The situation you describe is non-existant. Tournaments aren't being
> polayed with judges that are "hard to call", and the multi-judge rule
> ensures that there is always oversight in smaller events.

There are different levels of judge's support, as well as there are
different levels of reading skill, for instance. Theoretically, every
person can read after school, but if he has difficulties of reading
anything besides comics, you can say that he is effectively
illiterate. Similarly, every player can theoretically call a judge,
but if it takes serious efforts, then EFFECTIVELY there are no judge.
Yes, it may be an exaggeration, but not much.

> > Yes, he can. For a "bokkeeping judge" it would be "Call me if you
> > cannot solve the question yourself" :)
>
> By that description, no event I've ever attended had a "bookkeeping judge".

I'm very happy to hear that! But I wasn't the first to bring the word
"bookkeeper" into this discussion, it was a Finnish player. Hope that
things aren't that bad there, too.

> > I require the decklists for all my tournaments. And cannot see any
> > reasons to play without them.
>
> Reason #1: They are being selectively implemented in a fashion that
> artificially inflates the severity of the default penalty under 102 Illegal
> Deck (legal Decklist).

Let's prohibit kitchen knives, then! Reason #1: They were frequently
used to kill people :D

Decklists cannot be "guilty" of anything. They are just tools that
should be implemented properly.

> They're not doing in VTES what you think they are doing. There are a
> myriad of ways to arrive at accurate rulings quickly and efficiently
> without them, which is why so many can see no obvious reasons to play with
> them, either.

If you have decklists, then:
1). You can check every player's deck, should you need it. You aren't
forced to perform a deckcheck, but as long as your players know that
you can, they are going to be more careful with their decks.
2). You can help your players to restore their decks to their original
status, should the need arise.
3). By examining a decklist, you can evaluate whether some player is
violating PTW or not (i.e. whether he really has no reasonable chances
to get VPs or not) without meddling in the game.
4). Your chances to notice cheating is higher. Cheating with the deck
contents is obviously much more dangerous as long as the judge can
check your decklist any time, but other kinds of cheating may be
discovered, too. For instance, your chances to notice
Cheating:Collusion without meddling in the game are much higher if you
can examine the decklists.

Yes, it's possible to play without the decklists. They are the
"emergency tool", and you can be brave enough (or reckless enough) to
play without them. But they are well worth their price, and sometimes
they're really invaluable.

> > Even the most lazy of my players are
> > able to submit them.
>

You are angry without any reason. I'm happy that nobody can call you
lazy, but as long as you can handle your very intense job, your two
children and other duties, filling a decklist should be nothing to
you. I guess you have a printer and a deckbuilder program, so it's
going to take not more than 20-30 seconds of your precious time and
one sheet of paper. Not a large price for the advantages that
decklists provide (see above).
Do you have some emergency tools to protect your house, your family
and your property? I guess you do. Maybe, a fire extinguisher, an
insurance, or even a gun. All these things cost you some time and
money, but they are worth doing. Decklists work absolutely the same
way. They can protect only your tournament, not your house or family,
but they also cost you much, much less. Almost nothing, to be sure.
Even though you're a damned good VTES player, you still can lose some
cards from your deck (shit happens), and the decent judge will allow
you to use proxies if the cards are in your decklist.
If you're a judge, then you don't have to fill any decklists, so why
was all this fuss?

> > It was just a my commentary to the word "works". How can a judge be
> > sure that everything is OK, if he doesn't oversee the tables?
>

> the situaion Etherial describes, where theres a judge for every player.

> not-OK.

The players will alert the judge only if they realize that something's
wrong. This isn't always the case.
Yes, I cannot oversee all tables at once, but I'm doing my best to
quickly evaluate the situation at each table, and then I move to the
next one. Sometimes the situation is very complicated, so I have to
stay near the table for a while. My ultimate goal is creating the
impression that I'm always near, and with 4-5 tables I usually can do
it.

Yours,
Ector

it), the worst possible end result is after the event, somone
discovering the actual ruling and saying "hey--you got that wrong, it
actually goes like this...", and everyone moves on. And no one has to

identity of "judge", it isn't a big deal.

> ideal should not prevent us from attempting to reach the ideal :)

feel "shame" for getting a ruling wrong. I go "Oh, hey, what do you
know. Next time I'll get that right." and we move on. I'd prefer that I
got rules questions right, but as when I am running a tournament I
usually have 3 or 4 other judges to work with (one of the many
advantages of the "multi-judge" system), whenever there is a rules
question that is not readily apparent, there are enough opinions
available to figure out the actual answer most of the time.

Yes, it is possible. Although pretty unlikely, and very few people, if
any, would have done this. 'Cause most folks don't cheat, as it is

eyes. And if used for deck checks, they are just as likely to cause
unacceptable damage as not. And if they *aren't* being used for deck

playing around a table with some friends and playing at a tournament is

You create straw men all the time. All over this discussion. Left and

> it's obvious that the decklists help to notice some rules violations,
> and some people still insist on playing without them?

Holy crap. How did we get back here again? Decklists and deckchecks can
help notice some rules violations, yes. They can also unfairly punish
people for honest mistakes. And considering that the likelyhood of
someone intentionally cheating by changing their deck between rounds is
very low, and the likelyhood of then catching that person doing that
with random deck checks is very low, you are arguably *more* likely to
end up punishing someone for an innocent, honest mistake than you are to
actually catch someone cheating. How is this helping anything?

> Did you notice
> that somebody suggested dropping the decklists as a SOLUTION of the
> "hungarian problem"? This isn't even "tolerating" rules violations,
> this is completely ignoring them!

Not having decklists and deckchecks is not tolerating rules violations.
It is gambling on the incredibly high likelihood that there aren't going
to be any rules violations that decklists and deckchecks exist to
prevent.

If a rules violation becomes evident, even without decklists and
deckchecks, that rules violation is never tolerated. 'Cause cheating
isn't to be tolerated.

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
crispyfloss wrote:
>
> In my experience, no one has ever been deterred from asking a judge a
> question because the judge wasn't near by. In larger games, spread
> out across multiple rooms in a venue, we've paused a game for the 2 or
> 3 minutes it takes for someone to go find a judge to bring them back
> to ask a question. This hasn't ever been a problem.
How can you say that no one was deterred? In many cases, players have
their own opinion and call a judge just for a confirmation. In many
cases, they just refuse to call a judge if that appear to be
difficult. Surely, when they feel that they NEED a judge, they will
find him and wait until he arrives, but, unfortunately, they don't
always feel that way!

> I wouldn't rush to blame it on the judge in this case. After all, if
> he was near this table, wasn't he necessarily far from another table,
> which would then not have a judge near it?
I wanted to say that a good judge should create an impression that
he's ALWAYS near. If he is 3 metres away and watching the another
table, it isn't too far to call him for any reason. If he is 20 metres
away, and players cannot even see him, then he is too far away.

> > > This game is complicated. The interactions of so many cards
> > > frequently turn up with circumstances that players don't anticipate.
> > > Generally, if all players think something operates in a certain way,
> > > they're probably right.
> >
> > I've provided two examples when they were WRONG, and now you are
> > telling me the opposite.
>
> In the first case, it was a judge that was wrong, so that's not
> responsive to my point. If you were a player, and a judge issued a
> ruling that you knew was wrong, you would have to abide by it.
This wasn't my point. In the first example, nobody even called the
judge in the preliminary round! This was my real point.

> > For instance, Peter D. Bakija himself was mistakingly thinking that
> > Skin of Night can prevent Rotschreck - you can safely assume that
> > the less experienced players at his table going to believe his rulings.
>
> Regardless of who says it, If he's the one playing Rotschreck, I would
> be inclined to believe him, because he's saying something that harms
> him.
>
> If he's the one playing Skin of Night, then I wouldn't disbelieve him,
> but I'd want a judge to verify it because he's saying something that
> is beneficial to him.
Do you call a judge each time when a player says things that are
beneficial to him? I guess you don't, since such behaviour would spoil
the "friendly" atmosphere around you. I guess you're going to believe
that player, especially if you know him as a honest and experienced
player (like Peter, for instance). Thus, the improper ruling is going
to remain not fixed.
Besides, what if the "rule-monger" isn't one of those players, but
both players trust him as a more experienced player? This happens all
the time.
The only right way is: ask ONLY the judge, and the judge must be
ALWAYS near. After several tournaments, no player would even think
about solving such questions without a judge. Wonderful!
Note that Skin + Rot isn't a very complicated question - there are
much, much more complicated. And if somebody plays Jalan-Aajav or
Karsh that have "inbuilt" Skin of Night, such situation is very likely
to happen.

> So I'd call a judge over.
>
> Ironically, a less experienced player would probably trust a ruling by
> someone like Peter less than a more experienced player, since a more
> experienced player knows more of his reputation and has had more
> opportunities to see him exercise his judgment first hand.
People usually call a judge only if they doubt in something, and that
"something" really matters to them. There are many situations where
the "obvious" ruling is wrong, as in this case. Everyone can believe
that the vampire who treats aggravated damage as normal cannot be
affected by Rotschreck at all, even the experienced player. Why should
they call a judge if the experienced player already described
everything?
Again, the only solution is to ask ONLY the judge.

> > If any player isn't completely sure about some ruling, he can call the
> > judge if the judge is near. This never hurts. If the judge isn't near,
> > the player isn't going to look for him. Simply enough.
>
> This is the problem that everyone keeps referring to. As far as I can
> tell this discussion started as something like:
>
> Organizing, hands-off judges are horrible and watchful, hands-on
> judges are great.
>
> If you qualified this at the beginning with "Our players don't ask
> questions, so we need to keep an eye on them to make sure you're
> playing right," then everyone would understand where you're coming
> from. It's that you assume that everyone knows this, and then make
> statements that say you think it's true of everyone. Which, I think
> understandably, rubs people the wrong way.
People are different, but some "common" behaviour still can be
determined. I can easily believe that there are players that NEVER ask
another players and always look for a judge, but I don't think that
such behaviour can be common, since it wouldn't be the "friendly and
relaxed" game anymore. Also, keeping an eye on the players is always
good, since they can do stupid mistakes - yes, even the experienced
players can. And, really, there can be cheaters, too!

> > Any player can make a mistake about rules. Even the most serious one.
>
> Even a judge. And 5 good players will tend to give a better answer
> than 1 good judge.
Yes, a judge can make a mistake too. But the chance of his mistake
with the rules is much less than a chance of player's mistake (or 5
players' mistake, or even 100 players' mistake). Because judging the
game and playing the game require completely different skills. A
player may play for 10 years and encounter, say, 20 cases when he was
unable to provide an immediate ruling and was forced to look at the
NG. A judge may judge for one year and have more than a hundred of
such cases, because handling such cases is his job! So, a well-
experienced judge will almost never make mistakes about rules, but a
well-experienced player (even a champion) still can mistake.
Sometimes, ALL my players were confused about the rules, but I still
provided the correct ruling. Certainly, this happened in Magic, since
I'm not that good VTES judge (yet), but you should get the picture...

> And the reason some of us don't agree with what you say is that all
> judges are players, and prone to the same mistakes.
Well, you know, I never play in the tournament I'm judging, since I
don't believe in the "six-judges" even a single bit. This,
unfortunately, means that I play very rarely, and I'm a bad player.
But I hope to become a good judge instead, since we really need a good
judge.

> Pretending that a judge knows the rules well enough to make such cases
> impossible is just as naive.
Not "impossible" for sure, but "much more rare" is still good enough.

> Except, here's the thing: if you ask 5 players, the odds of a careless
> mistake goes down. The odds of seeing the right answer goes up. If
> you ask one judge, the odds of a careless mistake increases. Since
> careless mistakes are hard to see when you make them yourself.
Who is going to ask at all? Player is just playing the game without
noticing that he made a mistake. Other players are also playing the
game, and only the judge *specializes* on watching the game. Only the
judge isn't interested in the outcome, only the judge cares nothing
besides maintaining the order, and only his mind isn't filled with
game plans. That's why one judge has much better chances to notice the
careless mistake that all 5 players on the table.

> > Can you please tell me what of his reasons are "good" in your eyes?
> > VTES is "recreational" even at ECQ level? Players never cheat? Or
> > cheating with your deck isn't going to bring you any advantages? Or
> > something else?
>
> Cheating in this way doesn't give substantial advantages because it is
> a multiple-player game.
> The penalty is more likely to punish the innocent than the guilty.
> Individual cards simply aren't that powerful.
> Just accept this is an area where we disagree.
I agree that the current penalty is too harsh, but not with the other
statements. Cheating this way can give very substantial advantages,
and even if they appear to be minimal, it's still cheating and must be
punished. Some individual cards are extremely powerful - besides, who
said that a cheater cannot change 20 cards, not just one? If you're
playing without the decklists, the potential cheaters know that you
CANNOT catch them, so they can safely change 20 cards, or even more.
The right penalty for Illegal Deck should be something different
between a Warning (which would encourage cheaters) and a Game Loss
(which is too harsh for non-cheaters). Once again, a judge must use
his judgement, and issue only Warning for the lost Haven Uncovered,
for instance.

> > Nobody here feels that they are "on trial". But everybody knows that
> > the judge is near, and he isn't going to let the players cheat freely.
> > This really doesn't worry anybody, as we don't have the intentional
> > cheaters here (at least I believe so).
>
> That is what our judges do, too. Without deck lists.
Without the decklists you actually let your players to cheat with
their decks freely, since you have no way to catch possible cheaters.
Yes, you may think that your players don't cheat, as I do. But this
can be compared with an open door:
Do you leave your door open wide when you leave your place? I guess
not. You may think that there are no thieves in your neighbourhood,
but you cannot know this for sure, and *encouraging* stealing would be
just silly. So you have a door lock. You may realize that a well-
trained criminal is going to open your door in a second, but the lock
will deter the bad-trained ones or at least help to catch them (they
will be forced to spend some time on picking the lock or breaking in
the door)
Decklists do absolutely the same. You guess there are no cheaters, but
you cannot know this for sure (especially if you neved played with the
decklists). When you play without the decklists, you *encourage*
cheating, since they can get an advantage without any risk of being
caught. Again, a very good cheater can cheat even with the decklists,
but they will deter the poorly-trained or help the judge to catch
them.
So, why do you argue against the decklists, as long as you have the
door lock?

> Fair play makes the game fun.
>
> People don't play games to win - they play to win according to rules
> they agree to with other players.
You are talking about the GOOD players. But you cannot be sure that
ALL players are good. People are different, you know. While a good
player may have fun for trying to win according to the rules, a
cheater may have fun for winning WITHOUT the rules. Or even for the
very fact that he violated the rules and wasn't catched.

> > I feel like I'm talking with drug addicts or hippies! Is "making your

> > players happy" your only goal?
>

> Not the only goal, but a very important one. If people don't enjoy
> the playing the game, they won't play any more. The game is better
> the more players are in it, because it makes more interactions.
> Players enjoy the game because of the challenge. Players agree that
> the rules of the game are the best way to have that fun.
This is the major point of the discussion: what is more important -
"fun" or "order"? As long as you agree that there cannot be fun when
people violate the rules (i.e. without order), you are going to place
"order" over the "fun". Then it will be just logical to use decklists,
since they can really help to maintain order, and they almost never
spoil somebody's fun[0][1]. Simple enough?
Now you can start wondering why there are so many people here that
pretend to place "fun" over the "order", as I'm wondering from the
very beginning.

[0] A GL for illegal deck can really spoil the fun, but decklists
aren't "guilty" here. We simply need the new Judge's Guidelines.
[1] Somebody may pretend that filling the decklist and having to count
his cards after each game spoils the fun, but actually this takes
small amount of time, and it's beneficial for the player. Who likes to
play with incomplete deck?

> > Players must obey the rules, judges must enforce the rules and
> > maintain order. Players are usually happy within those borders, but
> > they cannot cross them. Penalties for rules violation are never going
> > to make people happy - are you suggesting to drop them at all?
>

> A penalty for a rules violation will make all the players that are
> following the rules happy. That's most of the players.
>
> And if a good, honest player that had done very well in original
> rounds had an extra Reunion Kamut in his deck or was missing a Secure
> Haven in his deck, and was disqualified from the finals on that basis,
> that would probably make more players unhappy than it made happy.
>
> Because that's seen as being unfair.
Trust me, I fully understand this attitude. And I would even feel the
same should I play at that tournament.
But let's answer to the two classical questions of Russian literature:
"Who is guilty?" and "What should be done?"
* Who is guilty here? Partially, the player is, since he wasn't
accurate enough with his deck (or his decklist). Does he deserve GL in
the finals? Probably not. So, is the judge guilty? He cannot be, since
he just followed the Guidelines. So, the Guidelines are "guilty" here.
* What should be done? Obviously, the Judge's Guidelines must be
reworked. A "VP Loss" would be an adequate penalty for such
infraction. Plus, they should recommend to check the decks as soon as
possible, not just wait for the finals and then discover the deck
problems.

This case has absolutely nothing common with the decklists usefulness
or "harmfulness". Should these players play the finals with the
illegal decks, it would NOT be a good solution. Actually, this would
be even worse.

> If in your group, people think that's fair, and want to catch those
> players, because otherwise they think they're being treated unfairly
> and therefore not having fun, then use decklists. Catch them. Punish
> them. But realize that we differ here, because it's what the players
> want.
Judges should NOT depend on what people think. This is just funny -
can you imagine a cop asking people: "What do you think - two years of
prison would be enough for him or not? Let's make a poll!"
Rules should be the same (or nearly the same) for all playgroups.
That's why we need a new Guidelines, too.

> > I know very well what does the "relaxed" atmosphere mean. No satanic
> > blood orgies, for sure, but no penalties for rules violation, either.
>
> Then you don't understand what we mean when we say "relaxed
> atmosphere." Because appropriate penalties for rules violations are
> the norm. We disagree on what's appropriate, but again, that's not
> disagreeing with the rules. Just how much punishment is appropriate,
> and therefore how much effort should be put into finding violations.
Looks like I really didn't understand what "relaxing atmosphere"
means, and, especially, why it was used as an argument against using
the decklists. Is there any player who cannot relax after filling a
decklist? More importantly, doesn't knowing that you can always use
your decklist to restore your deck to its original state make you MORE
relaxed?

> > Some rules violations would inevitably remain unnoticed, some rulings
> > provided by the players will inevitably appear to be wrong. As long as
> > I'm a judge, I cannot tolerate such things, and I'm obliged to do my
> > best to prevent them. Very simple, right?
>

> If you cannot tolerate such things.
>
> If your players want you to not tolerate such things.
Players are different. Some are going to tolerate almost everything,
as long as they are intact. Others really appreciate a good order.

> You don't have to justify your discretion to anyone here, you have to
> justify it to your players. It's why it's called discretion.
I never had much problems with my players. Most of the time they
believe my words, and I never issue penalties if I'm not sure that
they are deserved. They aren't disciplined enough, but I'm not a very
good judge, too...

Yours,
Ector

Ector <Ec...@mail.ru> wrote:

> Do you call a judge each time when a player says things that are
> beneficial to him? I guess you don't, since such behaviour would spoil

Fer fuck sake. There is a table full of people playing this game.
Between the lot of them, they know most of the rules. If someone says

Messages.Author: crispyfloss
Messages.Body:
Ector wrote:

> crispyfloss wrote:
> > I wouldn't rush to blame it on the judge in this case. After all, if
> > he was near this table, wasn't he necessarily far from another table,
> > which would then not have a judge near it?

> I wanted to say that a good judge should create an impression that
> he's ALWAYS near. If he is 3 metres away and watching the another
> table, it isn't too far to call him for any reason. If he is 20 metres
> away, and players cannot even see him, then he is too far away.

Our judges give that impression.

> > In the first case, it was a judge that was wrong, so that's not
> > responsive to my point. If you were a player, and a judge issued a
> > ruling that you knew was wrong, you would have to abide by it.

> This wasn't my point. In the first example, nobody even called the
> judge in the preliminary round! This was my real point.

If it mattered, and they didn't, they learned to do it next time.
Learning: it's where players that know the rules come from. Having
someone else learn for you: it's where players that always need a
judge around come from.

Okay, I understand your motivation now.

> > Regardless of who says it, If he's the one playing Rotschreck, I would
> > be inclined to believe him, because he's saying something that harms
> > him.
> >
> > If he's the one playing Skin of Night, then I wouldn't disbelieve him,
> > but I'd want a judge to verify it because he's saying something that
> > is beneficial to him.

> Do you call a judge each time when a player says things that are
> beneficial to him? I guess you don't, since such behaviour would spoil
> the "friendly" atmosphere around you. I guess you're going to believe
> that player, especially if you know him as a honest and experienced
> player (like Peter, for instance). Thus, the improper ruling is going
> to remain not fixed.

This is the "straw man" that others have referred to. You're assuming
something that ignores what I said, and then using it to make a
conclusion that I just responded to.

> Besides, what if the "rule-monger" isn't one of those players, but
> both players trust him as a more experienced player? This happens all
> the time.

If it's wrong, and they get the short end of the stick, they learn not
to trust people on things that matter. See above re: "learning."

> The only right way is: ask ONLY the judge, and the judge must be
> ALWAYS near. After several tournaments, no player would even think
> about solving such questions without a judge. Wonderful!
> Note that Skin + Rot isn't a very complicated question - there are
> much, much more complicated. And if somebody plays Jalan-Aajav or
> Karsh that have "inbuilt" Skin of Night, such situation is very likely
> to happen.

To throw your own question back at you: what do they ask questions
on? Everything? Everything beneficial to the other player? You need
to trust players to have some basic level of competence, and to know
that limit. Otherwise the only way to reach this "right way" nirvana
of yours is to have a judge watch everything that happens in each
game. See previous message re: "16% of your players have to be judge-
caliber, good luck with that."

> > Ironically, a less experienced player would probably trust a ruling by
> > someone like Peter less than a more experienced player, since a more
> > experienced player knows more of his reputation and has had more
> > opportunities to see him exercise his judgment first hand.

> People usually call a judge only if they doubt in something, and that
> "something" really matters to them. There are many situations where
> the "obvious" ruling is wrong, as in this case. Everyone can believe
> that the vampire who treats aggravated damage as normal cannot be
> affected by Rotschreck at all, even the experienced player. Why should
> they call a judge if the experienced player already described
> everything?

Your point has drifted to: players can't be trusted to know what they
don't know, and they will make horrible errors if they do something
wrong. Having a judge watch everything fixes this.

I expect you will find that even more players disagree with this point
(if it's different, feel free to clarify) than disagree with you on
decklists.

> People are different, but some "common" behaviour still can be
> determined. I can easily believe that there are players that NEVER ask
> another players and always look for a judge, but I don't think that
> such behaviour can be common, since it wouldn't be the "friendly and
> relaxed" game anymore. Also, keeping an eye on the players is always
> good, since they can do stupid mistakes - yes, even the experienced
> players can. And, really, there can be cheaters, too!

You think wrong. Asking for a judge is never seen as hostile. It's
just a question of knowing when is appropriate.

"Wow, that combination is really strong - I never thought it worked
that way! I'm going to ask a judge, because I always thought ..."

> Yes, a judge can make a mistake too. But the chance of his mistake
> with the rules is much less than a chance of player's mistake (or 5
> players' mistake, or even 100 players' mistake). Because judging the
> game and playing the game require completely different skills.

Being a good judge requires experience. Experience is gained by
playing, because you see how cards interact, you have questions come
up in bizarre combinations, and you see what might be too powerful
that might make you think you're doing it wrong.

> A player may play for 10 years and encounter, say, 20 cases when he was
> unable to provide an immediate ruling and was forced to look at the
> NG. A judge may judge for one year and have more than a hundred of
> such cases, because handling such cases is his job! So, a well-

Someone that reads the NG will almost never make mistakes about the
rule, someone that doesn't still can.

Since someone that reads the NG will see every single case that has a
ruling made; and be able to express an opinion; and have the person
that decides the rules tell them if they're right or not.

This is far more important than whether your "job" is to judge or
not. You only see as many hard cases as your players provide.
Experienced players provide fewer easy cases, and more hard cases.
Inexperienced players provide the opposite.

Which may be why you overstate the number of incidents that require
the keen watchful eye of the judge.

> > And the reason some of us don't agree with what you say is that all
> > judges are players, and prone to the same mistakes.

> Well, you know, I never play in the tournament I'm judging, since I
> don't believe in the "six-judges" even a single bit. This,
> unfortunately, means that I play very rarely, and I'm a bad player.
> But I hope to become a good judge instead, since we really need a good
> judge.

You can actually be a player and a judge but not both at the same
time. Really!

We don't have any professional judges. We have judges that have
played so much they really know this stuff.

I think you will find that playing more often - even if you're bad -
makes you a much better judge.

> > That is what our judges do, too. Without deck lists.

> Without the decklists you actually let your players to cheat with
> their decks freely, since you have no way to catch possible cheaters.
> Yes, you may think that your players don't cheat, as I do. But this
> can be compared with an open door:

It can be compared with not using decklists. Very effectively, in
fact.

I don't think someone walked off with my TV last time I left a secure
haven in their deck.

> > People don't play games to win - they play to win according to rules
> > they agree to with other players.

> > Not the only goal, but a very important one. If people don't enjoy

> > the playing the game, they won't play any more. The game is better
> > the more players are in it, because it makes more interactions.
> > Players enjoy the game because of the challenge. Players agree that
> > the rules of the game are the best way to have that fun.

> This is the major point of the discussion: what is more important -
> "fun" or "order"? As long as you agree that there cannot be fun when
> people violate the rules (i.e. without order), you are going to place
> "order" over the "fun". Then it will be just logical to use decklists,
> since they can really help to maintain order, and they almost never
> spoil somebody's fun[0][1]. Simple enough?

In a black/white world. Which we don't live in. Some amount of order
is necessary, some amount of fun is necessary. Some amount of fun
comes from having order. Some amount of resentment and frustration
comes from having too much. Like if you play 3 honest games and then
have to sit out of a final because someone else left a secure haven in
your deck.

> Now you can start wondering why there are so many people here that
> pretend to place "fun" over the "order", as I'm wondering from the
> very beginning.

You might wonder why so few agree with you.

Probably because we don't have such problems.

> > If in your group, people think that's fair, and want to catch those
> > players, because otherwise they think they're being treated unfairly
> > and therefore not having fun, then use decklists. Catch them. Punish
> > them. But realize that we differ here, because it's what the players
> > want.

> Judges should NOT depend on what people think. This is just funny -
> can you imagine a cop asking people: "What do you think - two years of
> prison would be enough for him or not? Let's make a poll!"

Judges have to depend on what people think, or people won't consent to
be judged by them.

I couldn't imagine a VTES judge comparing himself to law enforcement
and throwing people in prison until now, so there's something new for
both of us :-).

Messages.Body:

Hash: SHA1

Ector wrote:
> On Apr 19, 4:34 pm, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>> I think you generate a lot of preconceived notions and fantasies about this
>> topic, mostly in an attempt to justify what appears to be a very heavy
>> handed application of penalties, by VTES standards.
>
> OK, let's make some things clear.
> 3). I think that decklists never hurt, but can help sometimes.

This is the core of your mistake.

Requiring deck lists does hurt, because it annoys the shit out of many
players to have to fill them out in the first place.

Ector, I am now going to grant unto you a Fabulous Insight. Are you
ready? If you are capable of accepting this Insight, then you may
finally begin to understand why everyone is kicking you in the nuts over
this, and why you are just plain wrong.

YOU CAN NEVER CONTROL WHAT OTHERS THINK.

Oh my god. We better hear that one again.

YOU CAN NEVER CONTROL WHAT OTHERS THINK.

Wow, he really said it!

So what does it mean, Great Guru, what does it mean?

Well, what it means is:

If your players are annoyed at the hoops you're making them jump through
just to PLAY A GAME and HAVE SOME FUN, then sitting there on your high
horse and telling them "But you shouldn't feel that way" ...REGARDLESS
OF THE REASON... is not only inconsiderate, it's just plain fucking
stupid. It's even more plain fucking stupid when one of your primary
reasons is "to make it easier on me, the judge."

If you want your players to not be annoyed, then you have to make some
sort of effort to not annoy them. If deck lists are annoying your
players sufficiently, then you should consider how actually necessary
they really are. And what THAT all comes down to is: deck lists are not
necessary to play the game, run a tournament, or even hold a Continental
Qualifier. Therefore, rather than annoy the players for the convenience
of the judge, deck lists must go.

And it's that simple.

Oh, wait. You want me to spell out why it's bad to annoy players?
Annoyed players find something else to do with their spare time (in
which they had hoped to have fun), something that _is_, in fact, fun.
When players aren't playing the game, it is _always_ worse than when
they are, no matter what.

> 4). I don't believe that the judge can really rely on things like
> "players are friendly", "players know the rules" or something similar.
> In many cases, this appears to be wrong.

You made the part about "in many cases" up on the spot. You have no
idea about "many cases" because you have no experience outside Belarus.
All the tournaments ever played in Belarus aggregated together are not
even remotely enough to constitute "many cases".

This is why people don't respect you. You pretend to have a strict
moral code and then you resort to outright fabrication to support your
points.

> 5). I cannot agree that VTES isn't a sport game, at least at high-
> level tournaments like ECQ, EC and Nationals. You may call this a
> bias, if you wish.

No, I may call this outright stupidity.

Again, you cannot control what people think. Your desperate, insane
need to identify with a "serious" CCG and be recognized as a judge of
same does not change the facts.

People do not view V:TES as a serious game. They may play the game
seriously, with intent to win, but it is still all funsies at the end of
things. You cannot control this. You cannot declare what they "should"
think, just to make it match what you want to be true.

> b). Maniac prosecutor approach: "Aha! You were cheating! DQ!!!"
> c). My approach: "Attention everybody! Please be VERY careful with
> your decklists. Check them twice prior to submitting them. Also, check
> the number of cards in your deck after each round. You may get GL for
> illegal deck, so let's avoid that, OK?"

If you don't see how this is effectively the same as b), then you really
are as insane as Kevin says you are.

>> WHat do the other 3 players at the table do when Braggin Joe drops a wrong
>> ruling? In not-Belarus, any exploitation of rules questions to a player's
>> advantage over a newbie should be obvious to the others at the table, and
>> then a Judge would be called over.
> In most cases, the other 3 players (or 2 players at the 4-players
> table) are just not sure enough to say that Joe's ruling is wrong.

You made this up on the spot. You have no idea about "most" cases,
because your experience is entirely limited to Belarus. Your entire
argument is thus rendered null and void.

STOP FABRICATING EVIDENCE TO SUPPORT YOUR STATEMENTS.

- --
Derek

Ector wrote:
> On Apr 19, 5:28 am, Derek Ray
> <moot@idont_check_the_spamtrap_anyway.com> wrote:
>> Ector, the problem is that you do not know the difference.
>>
>> Could M:TG experience be helpful? Possibly. Could it hurt? We know at
>> least two ways in which it can, since you've mentioned two mistakes
>> you've made where you tried to apply M:TG concepts to V:TES.
>>
>> But you aren't even experienced enough to know when it'll help and when
>> it might hurt ... and that renders it useless.
>
> This isn't that simple. The more I know and the more VTES judging
> experience I get, the more useful my past Magic experience becomes.

And the more mistakes you make. Right now, in this thread, you have
made many, many mistakes. You are telling us that you are preparing to
make more mistakes in the future. And you think your Magic experience
is useful somehow?

> Especially considering the fact that Judge's Guidelines are minimal,
> and most judges aren't willing to use even those.

You made the part reading "most judges" up on the spot.

Don't fabricate evidence to support your arguments.

>>> BTW, does anyone think that football players are "rampant cheaters"?
>> First, I'm going to assume that you mean round-ball football.
>>
>> Second, yes, actually, diving is rampant in football, as are a number of
>> little pushes, shoves, knees, elbows, ... ALL outside the rules and all
>> of which should be called immediately. Why aren't they? The referee
>> cannot see because the offender is not close enough. So yes, I do think
>> football players are "rampant cheaters"; I just think that due to the
>> circumstances, both sides are permitted an equal opportunity to cheat,
>> so the game remains fair.
> No football judge would agree with such opinion.

How much would you like to bet me on that? I don't think you watch
football very much at all, and I am certain that you have never played
it, or this would not even be a topic of discussion.

> Players are supposed
> to play fair, and they are severely punished for violation of rules.

Not true. They are severely punished for violations of the rules that
the referee sees.

If the referee does not see the violation, he does not take the word of
the other team that a violation has occurred; he just warns everyone and
continues on, and penalizes the ones he does see.

> Sorry, but "permitted an equal opportunity to cheat" sounds just
> crazy. Are you going to say that the penalized players just exceeded
> that "allowed" opportunity to cheat?

They selected a poor time to cheat; while the referee was watching. Any
football player will tell you that... if you can win without cheating,
do so, but if you have to cheat, don't get caught.

> More importantly: why do you think that VTES players don't have "equal
> opportunity to cheat", too? This game also has its "little pushes,
> shoves, knees and elbows". You may look at the other player's hand,
> intentionally or not, you may "unintentionally" draw an extra card
> (and then put it back), and so on.

I don't think they don't have opportunity. I think they have no motive.

The game is played for fun. There are no enormous cash prizes at the
end; there's almost nothing, in fact. Only complete sociopaths cheat
just to cheat people. While the number of complete sociopaths who play
V:TES is assuredly greater than 0, my experience traveling across this
nation to multiple cities to play, combined with meeting the players who
have come here from Europe and Australia to play, combined with the
players I have conversed with in other locations on RGTCJ and IRC allows
me to be fully confident that it is also a number I can count on the
fingers of a single hand.

>> Note that this is different from the players not _wishing_ to call the
>> judge because they believe they can resolve the situation on their own.
>
> Yes, it's different. A judge should encourage players to ask him
> questions, not to "resolve on their own".

You meant to say "A judge should encourage players to ask him questions
if they have any doubts at all about the situation."

> If the players don't wish to
> call a judge, the judge should investigate why (after the tournament,
> of course). Maybe, he was too far away, or he was too busy? Maybe some
> people don't respect his knowledge? This is a serious problem for a
> person who wants to become a good judge.

However, the answer that is most common for "Why didn't you call a
judge?" is still "Because we didn't think we were wrong."

>> Because everyone was happy with the situation. As long is everyone is
>> playing by the same rules, even though the rules are incorrect, then the
>> game remains fair. No, really. Believe it, it's a fact.
>
> LSJ, are you reading this??? Do you think that it's normal and can be
> tolerated, too?

Of course it's normal. Ector, the fact that you don't play the game
really does affect your viewpoint here. You should play more and judge
less.

> I'm totally shocked with this. Any player that do everything, as long
> as he can convince the table to be happy :)

That "convincing the table" part that you gloss over here? Yeah, that's
a whole hell of a lot harder than it sounds.

Imagine this situation, where A preys on B on C on D on E.

A is a clueless newbie and makes a play.
B declares that the play is illegal because of "Y".

Do you really think that C is going to not speak up and call a judge if
he believes that B is providing wrong information? What about D and E?
And that doesn't even rule out A himself doing it.

No, Ector. If you are going to claim that it is easy to convince the
table to go along with any old hare-brained statement, then I must
correct you: you are wrong.

It is only easy to convince the table to go along with you when everyone
else agreed with you before you started convincing. If you played more,
you would know this.

>> You overestimate the desire for perfect, rigid order among players.
>> This is a game, Ector. It will never be more than a game. You are not
>> capable of making it more than a game; nobody is, but certainly not you.
>> It will always be a game.
>>
>> There will never be another Magic, or another Pokemon, or even (thank
>> god) another Yu-Gi-Oh. CCGs are a dying fad. People have moved on and
>> are doing other things now.
>>From my perspective, CCGs are still very popular, and their popularity
> is only increasing here.

Unfortunately, Belarus is not the marker by which an American-based
company will make its decisions on whether to continue printing cards
for a game that has long outlived its expected lifespan in a dying genre.

It is still a fact that V:TES will only be a game, and there is nothing
you will ever be able to do to change that. You need to accept it.

> And I really can't stand such words as "it's only a game". It's a
> GAME!!! You could say "It's only a life".

I take my life far more seriously than I do V:TES. I cannot imagine
losing my perspective on reality in such a fashion as to take V:TES
equally as seriously as I do with the rest of my life.

It IS only a game. I'm sorry that you are sufficiently unstable that
you cannot accept this. I recommend competent therapy, and an immediate
"cold turkey" quit from V:TES.

> Spending your time at the
> things that doesn't really matter to you isn't very clever. So,
> players that don't take the game seriously are going to leave, but the
> rest players will remain.

I don't ever want to play with players who think V:TES is on an equal
priority with the rest of their life. They are insane; dangerous to
themselves and others.

Life is life. Games are games. Confusing the two is a terrible,
terrible mistake.

>> People want to have fun. They want to play seriously to a certain
>> degree, as well. But they want to have fun, first and foremost. If
>> everyone at a table agrees that a play is correct and you are not
>> present to see the incorrect play, THAT IS OK. The players are all
>> still happy, and are having fun.
>
> People want to *win*, first and foremost.

False. For a few twisted souls, winning is the only path to fun. But
everyone else is playing to have fun, and their secondary goal is to win
(because, well, it _is_ more fun.)

> Having fun is great, as long as it doesn't prevent you from playing to
> win.

Correct. But in general, if someone is not having fun, then they will
not even play in the first place.

>> If someone is that concerned that the
>> 'correct' ruling be made, then they will call the judge over, trust me.
>> I can tell you from personal experience that US players have no fear of
>> saying "Let's get an official ruling on that. Hey, Judge!", and I doubt
>> that players in Belarus are much different.
>
> Yes, they can call a judge, if they feel that the judge is ready and
> willing to answer the questions.

Well, then there's no problem, right? Most of our judges over here are
both ready and willing to answer questions, and are usually to be found
within ten feet of the tournament playing area. I certainly was when I
judged, and I know all other judges who take pride in their ability also
are.

There have been poor judges in the past, but very very few, and none of
those people are still judges today... in some cases because there is no
longer a playgroup in that area. (Everyone quit the game.)

>> Sometimes, people will *gasp* play incorrectly, and nobody at the table
>> will notice. In the grand scheme of things, however, it just does not
>> matter. It is each player's responsibility to know the rules himself,
>> and to summon the judge for a ruling if he believes those rules have
>> been violated. If nobody summons the judge, nobody gets to complain
>> later "but that wasn't fair".
>
> This is false, which was demonstrated by LSJ himself when we discussed
> "correcting the game state". If you noticed that your vampire was
> improperly burned a turn ago, you still can call a judge, and the
> judge would have to correct the game state according to his judgement.

And that judgement might involve not restoring your vampire to play,
because too much has happened since then and it would be impossible to
rewind.

The statement remains true: if you don't summon a judge at the time the
question arises, you don't get to complain later. Or, more accurately
stated, you can complain all you want but you have no assurance that the
ideal remedy will be available.

>> The classic case of a Haven Uncovered being found in someone's vote deck
>> is, in fact, the best example here. It is obviously not the vote
>> deck's. It is easy to ask the player "Who was playing Havens on you?"
>> and confirm with the Archon that, in fact, the player he named was at a
>> previous table. Then you ask the named player if his deck is intact,
>> and sure enough, he will say "No, I'm missing a Haven". You restore
>> both decks to the correct state, issue a verbal warning to "be more
>> careful next time", and JUST. MOVE. ON.
>
> Yes, this is a decent way to resolve the problem if the HU was
> discovered between rounds. I never said that a player deserves a
> penalty for leaving HU. But every player is responsible for STARTING
> EACH ROUND with the same deck. What are you going to do if that voting
> deck player DRAW that HU during the game, for instance?

Find out whose deck it belongs to, put it in that player's ash heap,
issue the players involved a verbal warning ("be more careful"), and
move on. Oh, and make the vote deck's player draw another card.

Why does anything else need to happen?

Are you somehow under the delusion that the game was significantly
affected by the vote deck's player drawing a card that wasn't in his
deck? I can assure you it wasn't. If you played more, you would know this.

What about the player whose deck was short one Haven? That is almost
certainly a disadvantage; this problem is self-correcting, move on.

>> For fuck's sake, if you need an intermediate penalty between Warning and
>> Game Loss, then just ASSIGN ONE. Alternately, just issue a warning and
>> say "Next warning, for whatever reason, will be an automatic GL."
>
> I do this regularly. But issuing penalties without any guidelines is
> too much responsibility for a single man, IMHO. People shouldn't be
> punished without the law.

It's just a game. Stop worrying so much. It's not like a murder was
committed or anything.

>> My god, are you incapable of thinking for yourself?
>
> I always have my opinion. But it's just my opinion, not the sanctioned
> recommendation, and I need the LAW.

A simple "yes" would have been sufficient.

> Without the proper law, players
> are free to complain about the penalties being "too harsh" or "too
> weak". And the law should be logical, without issuing GL for illegal
> deck.

The players can complain all they want. If my penalties truly ARE too
harsh or too weak, it will become patently obvious in the magnitude and
number of complaints I receive, and I will ask another judge to go over
the rulings with me.

However, if the only person complaining is the person I ruled against, I
am most certainly going to turn a deaf ear.

>>> But the philosophy of
>>> these rules is the same for ALL CCGs, so I cannot see why Magic
>>> experience cannot help here.
>> Because you are wrong. The philosophy is NOT the same.
>
> At least it's explained in the same words. Why should it be different,
> then?

Because the rules are simply the guidelines by which the game is played.
The culture of the game and the individual players determine the
philosophy of the game.

>> Well, Ector, it's a fact. V:TES is both friendly AND recreational.
>> Even the tournaments. It won't ever be anything but, no matter how much
>> you try to make it.
>>
>> Don't like it? Better quit the game now.
>
> Our tournaments aren't "recreational" for sure. Players get really
> tired after them.

Eight hours of play is tiring, whether a tournament is purely for
recreation or life-or-death serious. This evidence does not support the
point you were hoping to make.

> And even if the tournaments are "friendly", that
> doesn't mean that tournaments are not sport events here. No need to
> quit the game for me.

It does, however, mean that you are taking this all far too seriously,
and making enormous mountains out of what really are just molehills.

>> No, Ector, you do not have to change the status quo. You have to admit
>> that you are wrong about this, have been wrong about this, and that you
>> will try to learn and apply that knowledge better next time.
>
> I'd sooner quit the game than admit that I'm wrong about this. Really.

Oops! Looks like there really IS a need for you to quit the game.

Because you _are_ wrong, you know. You've been wrong this entire
thread. You just refuse to admit it, even after multiple different
people have explained why you are wrong.

I don't think I've ever seen a more closed-minded person in my entire
life, honestly.

> You have your own way and pretend that it's the best way - me too. I
> don't think that my disciplined players will have any problems at the
> foreign tournaments, and I don't think that foreign players are going
> to have any serious problems here:
